domains.name: Mathematical Foundations
domains.summary: The mathematics that underwrites every learning algorithm: the linear and matrix structure of data, the calculus and optimization that turn objectives into weights, the probability and statistics that turn samples into belief, and the geometry, topology and complexity that bound what is learnable. This domain is deliberately deeper than typical bootcamp math, covering the tools (matrix analysis, concentration, information geometry, persistent homology) that separate practitioners who reason about models from those who merely call APIs.

subdomains.name: Linear Algebra and Matrix Theory
subdomains.summary: Matrix analysis, eigenvalue theory and the decompositions that recur throughout ML, including the non-negative and low-rank structure that bootcamps skip.

topics.name: Matrix Analysis and Eigenvalue Theory
topics.definition: Matrix analysis studies the qualitative behaviour of matrices and their eigenvalues under perturbation, ordering (Loewner), and functional calculus, treating a matrix as an operator rather than a bag of entries.
topics.explanation: Where a first course teaches how to compute eigenvalues, matrix analysis asks how they move when the matrix changes and which structural facts survive numerically. Central results are the Courant-Fischer min-max characterization, Weyl's inequalities and Mirsky's theorem for singular values, and the Hellmann-Feynman / first-order perturbation formulas that underlie sensitivity analysis. Matrix functions (exp, log, sqrt, inverse-power) are defined through the Jordan or Schur-Parlett calculus and are computed with Pade approximation and scaling-and-squaring rather than by diagonalizing. Non-negative matrices are governed by Perron-Frobenius theory, which guarantees a dominant real eigenvalue with a non-negative eigenvector and powers the PageRank vector, the stationary distribution of a chain, and spectral clustering. Normal, Hermitian and symmetric matrices admit orthogonal diagonalization with real spectra, while defective matrices need Jordan blocks; conflating the two is the classic error. This layer of theory is what makes covariance, Hessian and Laplacian spectra interpretable, which is why it sits ahead of most applied ML.
learning_objectives: State the Courant-Fischer min-max principle and use it to bound eigenvalues of a sum.
Apply Weyl and Mirsky inequalities to reason about eigenvalue and singular-value perturbations.
Define f(A) for analytic f via the Jordan and Schur-Parlett routes and explain scaling-and-squaring for exp(A).
Prove the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue exists for a primitive non-negative matrix and give a PageRank application.
Distinguish symmetric/Hermitian diagonalization from general Jordan form and know when eigen-decomposition is invalid.
math_foundations: Positive semidefinite cone and Loewner order
common_misconceptions: Every square matrix is diagonalizable (defective matrices need Jordan form).
Eigenvalue perturbation is always smooth (degenerate eigenvalues require the full min-max machinery).
exp(A) can be read off by exponentiating eigenvalues for a non-diagonalizable A.

further_reading.title: Functions of Matrices: Theory and Computation

topics.name: Matrix Decompositions and Low-Rank Approximation
topics.definition: A matrix decomposition rewrites a matrix as a product or sum of structured factors; low-rank approximation finds a rank-constrained matrix closest to it under a chosen norm.
topics.explanation: Decompositions are the working vocabulary of ML linear algebra: LU with partial pivoting for direct solves, QR for orthonormalization and least squares, Cholesky for positive-definite systems, eigendecomposition for symmetric operators, and the singular value decomposition (SVD) for arbitrary ones. The SVD is the keystone because the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem proves the truncated SVD is the optimal low-rank approximation in both spectral and Frobenius norms, which is exactly the objective behind PCA, matrix completion, and recommender systems. The theorem also justifies the energy-criterion heuristic for choosing rank. Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) adds a positivity constraint that yields parts-based, interpretable decompositions at the cost of a non-convex, only-locally-convergent objective. When matrices are large, randomized sketching approximates the column space with a Gaussian or Count-Sketch projection and gives probabilistic guarantees and near-optimal truncations at a fraction of the cost; this is the practical randomized-SVD used for big data. A learner must be able to move between exact factorizations and their numerically stable implementations, and to know which decomposition answers which question.
learning_objectives: Compute and interpret LU, QR, Cholesky, eigendecomposition and SVD and say which applies when.
Prove the truncated SVD is optimal for rank-k approximation (Eckart-Young).
Formulate PCA as a rank-k Frobenius projection and recover the covariance eigen-decomposition.
Explain NMF's multiplicative-update / alternating-least-squares schemes and their local-convergence caveat.
Derive the one-pass randomized SVD and state its error guarantee.
math_foundations: Column, row and null spaces; rank
common_misconceptions: Eigendecomposition and SVD are the same (they coincide only for normal matrices).
Truncated SVD minimizes only the Frobenius norm (it is optimal for the spectral norm too).
NMF is convex and always finds the global optimum.

subdomains.name: Calculus, Variational Methods and Tensor Algebra
subdomains.summary: The differential and integral calculus of fields and functionals, plus multilinear tensor algebra - the language of physics-informed ML and higher-order data structure.

topics.name: Vector Calculus and the Calculus of Variations
topics.definition: Vector calculus differentiates and integrates fields (gradients, divergence, curl, Laplacian); the calculus of variations finds the functions that extremize functionals rather than numbers.
topics.explanation: Ordinary optimization extremizes a real-valued function of finitely many variables; the calculus of variations extremizes a functional that maps a whole function or field to a scalar, which is the setting of optimal transport, physics-informed neural networks, and continuous-depth networks such as neural ODEs. The Euler-Lagrange equation is the stationarity condition, obtained by setting the Gateaux (first) derivative of the functional to zero, and the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations is what lets one pass from an integral condition to a pointwise differential equation. In vector calculus the div/grad/curl identities and the integral theorems (Green, Stokes, Gauss / divergence) govern conservative fields, Laplacians and the graph Laplacian, all of which recur in ML: the heat / diffusion operator underlies diffusion maps, and divergence-free and gradient-field structure matters in flow and diffusion models. De Rham's insight - that curl-of-grad and div-of-curl vanish - explains the Helmholtz decomposition. A learner should be fluent in differentiating under the integral sign and in functional derivatives, because variational inference and optimal transport are written in exactly that grammar.
learning_objectives: Derive the Euler-Lagrange equation from a first-order stationarity argument.
Compute the Gateaux derivative of a functional and distinguish it from a partial derivative.
State Green's, Stokes' and the divergence theorems and apply the Laplacian to graph and diffusion operators.
Use the fundamental lemma to justify passing from integral to pointwise conditions.
Explain the Helmholtz decomposition and why curl grad = 0 and div curl = 0.
common_misconceptions: Optimizing a functional is the same as optimizing its integrand pointwise (the Euler-Lagrange operator couples neighbours).
Every vector field is conservative (curl must vanish on a simply connected domain).
Boundary terms never matter in variational derivations (natural boundary conditions arise from them).

further_reading.title: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra: Vectors, Matrices, and Least Squares

topics.name: Tensor and Multilinear Algebra
topics.definition: Multilinear algebra generalizes vectors and matrices to tensors of arbitrary order and studies their mode-wise linear maps, decompositions, and contraction rules.
topics.explanation: A matrix is a second-order tensor; most data has more than two modes - color images, video, multi-way relational data, and weight matrices inside neural layers. Higher-order tensors bring genuinely new phenomena that matrices lack: rank is not unique (tensor rank and multilinear rank differ), best low-rank approximation need not exist (the variety of bounded-rank tensors is not closed), and most tensor quantities are NP-hard to compute. The practical core is the CP (candecomp / PARAFAC) decomposition and the Tucker / higher-order SVD (HOSVD) decomposition, which generalize the SVD, plus the n-mode product and tensor contraction written compactly with Einstein summation notation. Tucker models appear in multi-way recommender systems and factorized neural layers, and CP underlies latent-variable identifiability results that have no matrix analogue. Tensor networks (matrix product states) re-emerge in quantum-inspired ML compression. A learner should understand why the tidy matrix-SVD intuition breaks in higher order, and how to manipulate indices and modes without dropping terms.
learning_objectives: Define a tensor, its modes, and the n-mode / multilinear product.
State CP and Tucker/HOSVD decompositions and when each is preferred.
Explain why best rank-k tensor approximation may not exist while the Tucker case does.
Write einsum-style contractions and derive a gradient through a bilinear form.
Give an example where tensor rank exceeds matrix rank.
math_foundations: Basis, coordinate, and change-of-basis for matrices
common_misconceptions: CP rank and Tucker multilinear rank are the same number.
The set of rank-r tensors is closed, so a best approximation always exists (false for r >= 2).
Most tensor decomposition problems are polynomial-time like matrix SVD.

further_reading.title: Tensor Decompositions and Applications
further_reading.authors: Tamara G. Kolda and Brett W. Bader

subdomains.name: Optimization
subdomains.summary: Convex and non-convex theory, first- and second-order and constrained methods, stochastic approximation, splitting/ADMM, and distributed/federated optimization.

topics.name: Convex Optimization and Duality
topics.definition: Convex optimization minimizes a convex objective over a convex set, where every local optimum is global, and duality expresses the problem through supporting hyperplanes of its epigraph.
topics.explanation: Convexity is the property that makes most classical ML solvable with guarantees. The theory rests on convex sets and functions, the first-order characterization f(y) >= f(x) + grad f(x)^T (y-x), and the second-order condition on the Hessian when it exists. The conjugate / Fenchel-Legendre transform rewrites smooth functions (squared loss, log-sum-exp, negative entropy) in ways that expose their gradients and proximal operators. Lagrangian duality converts constraints into a saddle-point problem, and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions give necessary-and-sufficient optimality under Slater's constraint qualification, which is where strong duality (zero gap) enters. Many ML models are recognized as instances of conic programs: linear and second-order cone and semidefinite programs, with disciplined convex programming (CVXPY-style) letting users compose problems that a solver will certify. Understanding duality demystifies the SVM dual, regularized risk, and Fenchel-softmax losses. This topic is the foundation the more advanced optimization and learning-theory topics build on.
learning_objectives: Verify convexity of an objective via first- or second-order conditions.
Form the Lagrangian, derive dual functions, and state weak vs strong duality.
Write the KKT conditions and use them to identify support vectors.
Model ridge / lasso regression and the soft-margin SVM as convex programs.
Apply Fenchel duality to a composite objective f + g.
common_misconceptions: Duality gap is always zero (weak duality permits a gap absent Slater).
KKT conditions alone certify global optimality without constraint qualifications.
Every convex program is a linear program.

topics.name: First-Order, Proximal and Splitting Methods
topics.definition: First-order methods use only gradients/subgradients; proximal and splitting methods decompose a composite objective into smooth and nonsmooth pieces handled separately.
topics.explanation: Because most large ML objectives are sums f(x) + g(x) with one differentiable part and one structured-but-nonsmooth part (lasso L1, indicators of constraint sets), first-order methods dominate. Subgradient descent converges at rate O(1/sqrt(k)) for nonsmooth convex problems, while (proximal) gradient descent achieves the sharp O(1/k) rate; the difference is what accelerated (Nesterov) methods push toward O(1/k^2). The proximal operator prox_g(v) = argmin_x g(x) + (1/2t)||x - v||^2 is the workhorse: it yields soft-thresholding for L1 and projection for indicators, giving ISTA/FISTA for sparse problems. Splitting methods - Douglas-Rachford and ADMM - alternate proximal steps on dual variables and are the standard tool for distributed, constrained, and consensus problems, which is why ADMM underlies decentralized model fitting. Mirror descent generalizes gradient descent to non-Euclidean geometries via a Bregman divergence (KL for the simplex, giving exponentiated-gradient and online-learning algorithms). This topic turns the abstract convex duality of the previous one into actual, deployable solvers.
learning_objectives: Compute proximal operators for L1, indicators, and log-barrier.
Derive the O(1/k) rate of gradient descent vs O(1/sqrt(k)) of subgradient descent.
Implement FISTA and state the Nesterov momentum scheme.
Write ADMM updates for a consensus problem and explain dual ascent.
Show that mirror descent with KL geometry is exponentiated-gradient.
common_misconceptions: Subgradient descent gets the same rate as smooth gradient descent (it is slower without strong convexity).
ADMM always converges to the true constrained optimum (fails without closed-prox / convexity).
Nesterov acceleration is just heavier momentum (the gradient is evaluated at a lookahead point).

further_reading.authors: Stephen Boyd, Neal Parikh, Eric Chu, Borja Peleato, Jonathan Eckstein

topics.name: Second-Order, Quasi-Newton and Trust-Region Methods
topics.definition: Second-order methods use curvature (Hessian or Gauss-Newton) to obtain superlinear convergence; quasi-Newton methods build curvature models from gradient differences without forming the Hessian.
topics.explanation: Newton's method solves the quadratic model exactly and converges quadratically near a nonsingular minimum, but forming and factorizing the Hessian is O(d^3) and the model can be wrong far from the optimum. Two families fix this: line-search and trust-region globalization. A trust-region method minimizes the local model inside a radius-1 step whose radius is adjusted by how well the model matches the function (the rho ratio), giving global convergence to second-order stationary points, which is the right notion in non-convex ML. Quasi-Newton methods approximate curvature from successive gradients: Broyden's rank-one update and the BFGS / limited-memory L-BFGS family maintain a positive-definite approximation with only O(d) memory, making L-BFGS the standard for medium-scale deterministic optimization, while SR1 handles indefinite curvature. Newton-Krylov and matrix-free methods combine inexact Newton with conjugate-gradient solves (Hessian-vector products) for large-scale or PDE-constrained problems. Natural gradient in statistics and Gauss-Newton in least-squares (Levenberg-Marquardt damping for robust fitting) are second-order methods in disguise. This topic is what a learner needs before trusting non-convex optimization analysis.
learning_objectives: Derive BFGS and its limited-memory L-BFGS recursion and the Sherman-Morrison update.
State the trust-region radius update rule via the model-vs-actual ratio rho.
Explain why Gauss-Newton drops the Hessian's residual term and when it is valid.
Contrast line-search vs trust-region globalization and their convergence rates.
Use natural gradient as a Fisher-metric second-order method.
math_foundations: Quadratic models and completing the square
common_misconceptions: Newton's method always converges without globalization (it diverges without line search or a trust region).
BFGS handles indefinite curvature (it requires the curvature condition s^T y > 0; use SR1 otherwise).
Quasi-Newton methods are equivalent to plain gradient descent.

further_reading.authors: Jorge Nocedal and Stephen J. Wright

further_reading.title: Trust Region Methods
further_reading.authors: Andrew R. Conn, Nicholas I. M. Gould, Philippe L. Toint

topics.name: Non-Convex Optimization and Landscape Analysis
topics.definition: Landscape analysis studies the geometry of non-convex objectives, characterizing their stationary points (minima, maxima, saddle points) and the algorithms that escape saddles to reach good minima.
topics.explanation: Most neural-network objectives are non-convex and high-dimensional, so the old fear of local minima is the wrong picture. In high dimension, random smooth functions overwhelmingly have saddle points rather than strict local minima, and the question becomes whether gradient-based methods can escape saddles. Lee, Jordan and Recht proved that strict saddle points (stationary points with at least one negative Hessian eigenvalue) are almost never a limit point of perturbed gradient descent, so first-order methods converge to second-order stationary points. The Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality give gradient-descent convergence to global minima without convexity, which explains benign over-parameterization regimes: the loss surface of wide networks is connected at the level set of a given loss value, and no spurious bad minima persist. Saddle-point structure matters in GANs and minimax objectives, where gradient descent-ascent can cycle around saddles and need extra machinery (negative-curvature directions, alternating updates). This topic is the theoretical justification for why 'any local minimum looks good' works in practice, and is a genuine frontier.
learning_objectives: Classify stationary points via the Hessian spectrum (minima, maxima, saddles).
Define a strict saddle and explain why perturbed GD almost surely escapes it.
State the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition and derive linear convergence under it.
Explain why saddle points dominate local minima in high dimensions.
Discuss the limits: not every non-convex problem is this benign.
common_misconceptions: Non-convex optimization is hopeless because of local minima (saddles dominate in high dimension).
PL / second-order results mean SGD always finds the global optimum (they bound stationarity, not optimality).
Gradient descent will generically get stuck at a saddle (measure-zero attraction under perturbation).

further_reading.authors: Yann N. Dauphin, Ronan Collobert, Corinna Cortes

further_reading.authors: Jason D. Lee, Max Simchowitz, Michael I. Jordan, Benjamin Recht

topics.name: Stochastic Approximation and SGD Theory
topics.definition: Stochastic approximation finds roots or optima of a function known only through noisy evaluations; SGD is its minimization form and the backbone of all large-scale training.
topics.explanation: Robbins and Monro introduced stochastic approximation in 1951 as an iterative root-finding scheme x_{k+1} = x_k - a_k * noisy-estimate, and the classical convergence condition sum a_k = infinity together with sum a_k^2 < infinity (stepsizes decaying like 1/k) is the precise reason the learning-rate schedule of SGD is shaped the way it is. The proof is a martingale convergence argument: the gradient noise forms a square-integrable martingale difference sequence whose sum is controlled, leaving a deterministic descent term. Polyak-Ruppert averaging of the iterates sharpens convergence to the optimal asymptotic variance, and decoupled averaging enables warm restarts (SGDR). Beyond plain SGD, the theory covers momentum (heavy ball and Nesterov), variance-reduction schemes such as SAGA and SVRG that recover linear rates by storing per-sample gradients, and adaptive methods (Adam, Adagrad, second-moment normalization) whose convergence properties differ from what practitioners assume. The connection between stepsize decay and concentration of measure, and the noise-vs-signal trade-off, explain batch-size scaling laws. This topic is the mathematical core of every optimizer a learner will use.
learning_objectives: State the Robbins-Monro stepsize conditions and why 1/k satisfies them.
Sketch the martingale-based convergence proof for SGD on convex objectives.
Derive Polyak averaging and explain its variance benefit.
Explain SAGA/SVRG variance reduction and where it applies (finite sums).
Characterize momentum and heavy-ball dynamics, and Adam's update.
common_misconceptions: SGD only works because of luck or small batch size (it works because of martingale convergence under stepsize decay).
Momentum is 'inertia' in a literal physical sense with no damping trade-off.
Adaptive optimizers always dominate SGD in rate (they can fail to converge on some problems).

further_reading.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent Performs Bayes Posterior Adaption

topics.name: Distributed and Federated Optimization
topics.definition: Distributed optimization solves a global objective split across machines or agents, coordinating either through shared parameters (parameter server) or local communication on a network; federated optimization does this under data privacy and heterogeneity constraints.
topics.explanation: As datasets exceed one machine, the objective decomposes into a sum of local terms f_i, and one must minimize it across devices. Data-parallel synchronous SGD and its parameter-server / ring-allreduce variants trade communication against waiting; decentralized consensus methods (D-PSGD, EXTRA) replace the central server with neighbors exchanging gradients, governed by the second eigenvalue of the communication graph. Federated averaging (FedAvg) runs local SGD between periodic aggregations, drastically reducing communication but degrading when client data is statistically heterogeneous (non-IID), which is precisely the dataset-shift problem. The central research questions are communication complexity (how many bits to reach a target accuracy), the effect of partial participation and stragglers, and privacy - aggregation plus secure sketching is not the same as differential privacy, a frequent misconception. Compression (sparsification, quantization) of messages with error-feedback lets the network bottleneck not dominate convergence. This topic ties optimization to graph theory and to real ML-systems concerns, and feeds directly into the domain-2 federated-learning topic.
learning_objectives: Derive the convergence dependence of decentralized SGD on the graph spectral gap.
Describe FedAvg's local-then-aggregate loop and the effect of non-IID data.
Distinguish synchronization (parameter server, ring allreduce) from decentralized gossip.
Explain error-feedback and compression schemes for communication reduction.
Separate 'federated' privacy benefits from formal differential-privacy guarantees.
math_foundations: Convergence of sums of random variables
common_misconceptions: Federated learning guarantees privacy by construction (aggregation alone leaks information; needs DP).
More local steps always helps (hurts convergence under heterogeneity).
Decentralized consensus needs a global broadcast every step.

subdomains.name: Numerical Analysis and Automatic Differentiation
subdomains.summary: The numerical reality behind exact math: floating-point conditioning, iterative solvers, and the mathematics and stability of automatic differentiation.

topics.name: Numerical Linear Algebra and Stability
topics.definition: Numerical linear algebra studies how to solve linear problems in finite precision: conditioning, floating-point error, algorithmic stability, and iterative solvers for large systems.
topics.explanation: Every exact linear-algebra identity degrades under machine precision, and whether it degrades gently or catastrophically is a separate question from the mathematical conditioning of the problem. The condition number kappa(A) = ||A|| ||A^{-1}|| bounds relative output error given relative input error; a well-conditioned problem can still be solved badly by an unstable algorithm. Floating-point arithmetic (IEEE 754) has finite machine epsilon, and the enemy is catastrophic cancellation when subtracting nearly equal numbers, while a stable algorithm guarantees backward stability - it solves a nearby exact problem. For large or sparse systems, direct factorization (LU, Cholesky) is O(n^3) memory-bound; iterative Krylov methods - conjugate gradient for symmetric positive-definite, GMRES for general, MINRES - exploit structure and matrix-vector products alone, with convergence driven by the clustering of the spectrum, and preconditioning (diagonal, incomplete Cholesky/ILU) reshapes the spectrum to accelerate them. These solvers appear when normal equations, Newton systems, and kernel-matrix solves are too big for exact factorization, and they are the prerequisite for understanding randomized SVD and matrix-free optimization.
learning_objectives: Define and bound conditioning and distinguish it from algorithm stability.
Explain machine epsilon and demonstrate catastrophic cancellation.
Characterize CG convergence in terms of the eigenvalue distribution of SPD matrices.
Construct a preconditioner and explain why it helps convergence.
Reason about when to use direct vs iterative solvers.
common_misconceptions: A small condition number guarantees a numerically accurate result (the algorithm must also be stable).
Normal equations are always fine (they square the condition number).
Iterative solvers converge slowly regardless of spectrum.

further_reading.title: Numerical Linear Algebra
further_reading.authors: Lloyd N. Trefethen and David Bau III

further_reading.title: Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms

topics.name: The Mathematics of Automatic Differentiation
topics.definition: Automatic differentiation computes exact derivatives of a program by systematically applying the chain rule to its elementary operations, as forward or reverse accumulation.
topics.explanation: Automatic differentiation is neither numerical differentiation (finite differences) nor symbolic algebra: it evaluates the chain rule by decomposing a program into a graph of primitives. Forward mode propagates tangent vectors (Jacobian-vector products, JVP) and costs O(d) per input derivative, making it efficient when the number of inputs is small; reverse mode propagates cotangents (vector-Jacobian products, VJP) and computes one scalar output's gradient in O(cost of evaluation), which is why it is the default for optimization and backpropagation. The 'adjoint method' is reverse mode in disguise. A crucial and often-missed subtlety is numerical stability: forward and reverse modes can accumulate different round-off, gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory but re-evaluation can produce non-identical round-off (and wrong adjoints if operations are nondeterministic), and second-order AD (Hessian-vector products) is numerically fragile. Differentiating through loops, conditionals, and implicit solvers (implicit function theorem) requires care. This topic is the precise mathematical content under the cross-area 'backpropagation' slug and explains why autodiff, not finite differences, is used at scale.
learning_objectives: Derive forward (tangent) and reverse (adjoint) mode from the chain rule on a DAG.
Count the computational complexity of a gradient in reverse mode.
Explain why reverse mode has better round-off behavior for scalar-valued functions.
Differentiate an implicitly-defined function using the implicit function theorem.
Describe gradient checkpointing and the determinism pitfall in re-evaluation.
common_misconceptions: Automatic differentiation = finite differences (it produces derivatives exact to machine precision).
Automatic differentiation = symbolic differentiation (no expression blowup).
Reverse-mode AD is free of numerical issues (nondeterminism and recompute can corrupt gradients).

subdomains.name: Probability and Stochastic Processes
subdomains.summary: Measure-theoretic probability, martingales, Markov chains and stochastic processes, high-dimensional concentration, and optimal transport - the probability machinery ML actually depends on.

topics.name: Measure-Theoretic Probability and Martingales
topics.definition: Probability formulated on sigma-algebras and measures, with expectation as a Lebesgue integral; martingales are processes whose conditional expectation is constant in time.
topics.explanation: A probability space is a measure space with total mass 1, and Kolmogorov's axioms make independence, conditioning, and expectation rigorous even for continuous and high-dimensional variables. The Lebesgue/Radon-Nikodym view of density, absolute continuity, and mutual singularity explains why likelihood ratios exist only when one measure dominates another - directly relevant to density-ratio estimation and domain adaptation. Expectation is an L1 integral, so the convergence theorems (monotone and dominated convergence, Fatou) are the justification for interchanging limits and expectations in learning-theory proofs. Modes of convergence (a.s., in probability, in distribution, in Lp) and the law of large numbers and central limit theorem form the probabilistic backbone of statistics. Martingales model the running conditional expectation and power the analysis of stochastic approximation and online learning; the martingale convergence theorem, Azuma-Hoeffding and the optional stopping theorem are the workhorses behind concentration arguments. This topic earns its measure-theoretic depth because it is exactly the vocabulary used in the learning-theory and stochastic-optimization proofs.
learning_objectives: Define probability, sigma-algebra, filtration, and conditional expectation rigorously.
Use Radon-Nikodym to construct a density from a dominating measure.
Apply monotone/dominated convergence to justify exchanging limits and integrals.
Prove the martingale convergence theorem's conditions and state Azuma-Hoeffding.
Distinguish the four modes of convergence and their implications.
common_misconceptions: Independence always implies a product-measure factorization (needs the sigma-algebra framing).
Conditional expectation is a fixed number (it is a random variable w.r.t. the conditioning sigma-algebra).
Dominated convergence applies without the domination condition.

further_reading.title: Introduction to Probability
further_reading.authors: Dimitri P. Bertsekas and John N. Tsitsiklis

topics.name: Markov Chains and Stochastic Processes
topics.definition: A Markov chain is a memoryless stochastic process on a state space; stochastic processes generalize this to include continuous-time and non-Markovian evolution.
topics.explanation: The Markov property - the future depends only on the present - collapses a complex joint process into a transition matrix, and the entire qualitative behavior is encoded in its spectrum and connectivity. Irreducibility, aperiodicity, and positive recurrence guarantee a unique stationary distribution, and the chain converges to it at a geometric rate governed by the spectral gap of the transition matrix. This is exactly the analysis behind Markov chain Monte Carlo (which samples from a desired stationary distribution via a designed chain), PageRank, and the stationary behavior of queueing systems. Continuous-time chains, Poisson processes, and birth-death processes extend the framework, and coupling plus total-variation mixing-time bounds quantify how many steps suffice for the chain to look stationary. In machine learning these chains underlie graphical-model samplers, random-walk embeddings, deep-walk / node2vec graph representations, and the SDE view of SGD. Understanding ergodicity and mixing also clarifies when a chain fails to converge because of periodicity, and why a spectral view of 'how fast do we forget the initialization' matters for sampler diagnostics. This topic is the entry point to the domain's Monte Carlo cross-area slugs.
learning_objectives: State irreducibility, aperiodicity, and recurrence and link them to a stationary distribution.
Compute a stationary distribution via the left eigenvector of the transition matrix.
Bound mixing time in total variation using the spectral gap.
Explain the coupling argument for convergence.
Connect Poisson and birth-death processes to queueing and MCMC proposals.
common_misconceptions: Any transition matrix has a unique stationary distribution (periodic / reducible chains may not).
MCMC samples converge to the wrong chain by accident - detailed balance fixes the target.
Mixing time is irrelevant when samples eventually look right (rate determines diagnostics).

further_reading.title: Markov Chains and Mixing Times
further_reading.authors: David A. Levin, Yuval Peres, Elizabeth L. Wilmer

topics.name: High-Dimensional Probability and Concentration
topics.definition: High-dimensional probability studies how random quantities behave as the ambient dimension grows with the sample size, focusing on concentration of measure and uniform bounds over large function classes.
topics.explanation: Modern ML operates where the number of parameters exceeds the number of samples, and the low-dimensional intuition that averages are close to expectations fails when you must be uniformly correct over exponentially many hypotheses. Concentration inequalities - Chernoff/Hoeffding/Bernstein - bound the probability that a sum of independent variables deviates, with sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential tails matching bounded and heavy-tailed noise, respectively. The crucial move is a union bound over an epsilon-net of the parameter space, leading to generic chaining and Dudley's entropy integral that bounds the supremum of a stochastic process by an integral of covering numbers, which is the quantitative engine behind Rademacher-complexity generalization bounds. Matrix concentration (matrix Bernstein, and the noncommutative Khintchine inequality) controls the spectral norm of a sum of random matrices, giving finite-sample bounds on the operator norm of a sample covariance, the empirical Fisher, or a random feature Gram matrix. The Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality, with its tight constant, gives a uniform bound on the deviation between empirical and true CDF, the basis for KS tests and distribution-free risk guarantees. Random projections and the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma compress dimension while preserving distances, underpinning sketching. This topic is what makes learning-theory bounds honest.
learning_objectives: Distinguish sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential tails and when each applies.
Prove a union bound over a finite class and convert it to an epsilon-net bound.
Apply matrix Bernstein to bound ||sample covariance - true covariance|| in spectral norm.
State the DKW inequality and explain its role in uniform CDF bounds.
Derive the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma and explain why it enables sketching.
common_misconceptions: Hoeffding gives the tightest bound (it is distribution-free; Bernstein uses variance).
Concentration over a fixed hypothesis automatically holds over a large class (need uniform/net arguments).
JL works for infinite sets without care.

further_reading.title: High-Dimensional Probability: An Introduction with Applications in Data Science
Concentration Inequalities: A Nonasymptotic Theory of Independence
further_reading.authors: Stephane Boucheron, Gabor Lugosi, Pascal Massart

topics.name: Optimal Transport and Wasserstein Geometry
topics.definition: Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to move one probability distribution into another; Wasserstein distances metrize weak convergence plus moments and give distributions a genuine geometric structure.
topics.explanation: Classical probability metrics like total variation and KL cannot even compare a continuous distribution to a point mass and ignore the geometry of the underlying space. The Monge formulation of transporting mass by a deterministic map and the Kantorovich relaxation via couplings make this precise, and Kantorovich duality expresses the transport cost as a supremum over pairs of potentials. The Wasserstein-p distance, W_p, is the optimal cost and is sensitive to the metric on the support: moving a Gaussian by 1 unit costs 1, not infinity, which is why W_2 works for measures with disjoint support where KL fails. Entropic regularization replaces the hard coupling with a smoothed one solved by Sinkhorn iterations, reducing the computational bottleneck to matrix scaling and giving fast, differentiable Wasserstein estimates. 1D transport reduces to quantile matching, the basis for normalizing flows and quantile normalization. Applications include comparing probability measures (generative models), domain adaptation, and generative modelling such as Wasserstein GANs and gradient-flow training of diffusion models. In information geometry, Wasserstein has a Riemannian structure; the Brenier map and displacement interpolation are the analogues of straight lines. This is one of the fastest-growing areas in modern ML.
learning_objectives: State the Monge and Kantorovich formulations and the transport-cost infimum.
Derive Kantorovich duality and identify optimal potentials.
Compute W_2 for Gaussian distributions in closed form.
Describe Sinkhorn / entropic-OT updates and their numerical behavior.
Explain why KL fails on disjoint support but Wasserstein does not.
common_misconceptions: KL divergence is a metric and works between any two distributions (fails on disjoint support).
Wasserstein has no closed form except numerically (it does for Gaussian and 1D cases).
Sinkhorn exactly solves OT (it solves a smoothed relaxation).

subdomains.name: Statistics and Inference
subdomains.summary: Frequentist and Bayesian estimation, minimax decision theory, multiple-testing and post-selection validity, and experimental design - the statistics ML evaluation quietly relies on.

topics.name: Statistical Decision Theory and Minimax Estimation
topics.definition: Decision theory evaluates estimators and rules by their risk under a loss function; minimax seeks the rule minimizing the worst-case risk over a parameter class.
topics.explanation: Every learning objective secretly chooses a loss, and decision theory makes that choice rigorous. An estimator maps data to a parameter; its risk is the expected loss, integrated over the sampling distribution. Admissibility (no other estimator dominates it everywhere), the complete-class theorems (Bayes rules and their limits are all you need consider), and the invariance / equivariance principles reduce infinite search spaces to small families such as least-squares and MLE. The minimax value is the best worst-case guarantee, and matching upper and lower bounds on it is the core of modern learning theory. Lower bounds are proved by packing arguments and Le Cam's two-point and Fano's inequalities, which reduce estimation difficulty to how many well-separated hypotheses the data can distinguish; these are exactly the tools used to prove nonparametric regression and density-estimation rates. Bayes estimators with a prior and the Stein effect (the admissibility of the James-Stein shrinkage estimator in dimension >= 3, showing the sample mean is inadmissible) teach that 'obvious' estimators can be dominated. James-Stein is the conceptual ancestor of ridge / shrinkage regularization, tying this topic directly to ML.
learning_objectives: Define risk, bias-variance decomposition under a loss, and admissibility.
State a complete-class theorem and explain why Bayes rules suffice.
Apply Le Cam's two-point and Fano methods to sketch a lower bound.
Explain the James-Stein phenomenon and connect it to shrinkage.
Relate minimax rates to sample-complexity lower bounds in learning.
common_misconceptions: The unbiased / maximum-likelihood estimator is always optimal (James-Stein shows it can be dominated).
Minimax and Bayes always agree (they coincide only along a least-favorable prior).
A lower bound on risk needs no hypothesis-packing argument.

further_reading.title: Theory of Point Estimation
further_reading.authors: E. L. Lehmann and George Casella

further_reading.title: Statistical Decision Theory and Bayesian Analysis

topics.name: Inference, Multiple Testing and Experimental Design
topics.definition: Classical inference estimates parameters and tests hypotheses with controlled error rates; multiple testing and post-selection inference keep those rates honest when many hypotheses are tried; experimental design plans data collection to make inference efficient.
topics.explanation: Machine-learning evaluation is applied statistics, and it is frequently done wrong. Point and interval estimation rest on MLE asymptotics (consistency and Fisher-information normality) and likelihood-ratio / Wald / score tests; exponential-family structure and the Fisher-Neyman factorization give sufficient statistics and make these tests clean. The problem is multiplicity: trying 20 configurations and reporting the best inflates the false-positive rate, so one must control the family-wise error rate (Bonferroni, Holm) or, more powerfully, the false discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) when screening many models or features. Post-selection and 'winner's-curse' bias arise precisely because the same data selected and then evaluated the model; selective inference (conditioning on the selection event, or using sample splitting / cross-fit inference) repairs the p-values and confidence intervals that naive reporting corrupts. This is central to honest benchmarking, model ablations, and feature-selection significance. Experimental design closes the loop: choosing where to sample / which arms to test, D-optimal and related criteria, and power analysis maximize information per sample, and active learning is its sequential, model-coupled relative. A practitioner who can run an A/B test and a model ablation without fooling themselves is doing this topic.
learning_objectives: Construct MLE / likelihood-ratio tests and quote their asymptotic null distributions.
Explain FWER vs FDR and apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.
Describe why selecting then testing the same data biases inference and how to fix it.
Use a D-optimality criterion and compute sample size for a target power.
Recognize exponential-family sufficient statistics and the Neyman factorization.
common_misconceptions: A p-value after selecting the best of 50 models is valid (selection biases it; needs correction).
BH controls the family-wise error rate (it controls the false discovery rate).
More parameters always means more power in design (variance vs bias trade-off governs).

further_reading.title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing
All of Statistics: A Concise Course in Statistical Inference

subdomains.name: Information Theory and Encoding
subdomains.summary: Shannon information, divergences and channel capacity, and the algorithmic-information / minimum-description-length view of learning as compression.

topics.name: Information Theory and f-Divergences
topics.definition: Information theory quantifies uncertainty and communication limits through entropy, mutual information and channel capacity; f-divergences generalize KL as a family of distribution distances.
topics.explanation: Shannon entropy H measures the average surprise of a distribution, cross-entropy its coding cost under a mismatched code, and relative entropy (KL divergence) the redundancy / expected log-likelihood-ratio between them, with the log-sum inequality giving the data-processing inequality that underlies the fact that post-processing cannot increase information. Mutual information I(X;Y) is the symmetric measure of dependence and is the objective in information bottleneck, feature selection, and independent component analysis; it connects entropy to the capacity of a noisy channel via the coding theorems. The f-divergence family (KL, reverse KL, total variation, Hellinger, chi-squared, alpha divergences, Jensen-Shannon) all arise from convex generators f and differ critically in their zero-avoiding vs mass-covering behavior, which dictates whether variational inference uses forward or reverse KL and why f-GAN objectives vary. The maximum-entropy principle says the least-committal distribution matching constraints is the exponential-family member with those sufficient statistics, which explains why logistic regression, softmax, and graphical models all land on exponential families. Information geometry turns KL into a Riemannian + dual-flat structure, foreshadowing the natural-gradient topic.
learning_objectives: Derive entropy, cross-entropy and KL and their coding interpretations.
Prove the data-processing inequality via the log-sum inequality.
Compute mutual information and relate it to the information bottleneck.
Explain forward vs reverse KL behavior and its consequence for inference.
State the max-entropy characterization of exponential families.
common_misconceptions: KL divergence is symmetric (it is not; reverse KL differs behaviorally).
Mutual information equals correlation (it captures nonlinear dependence too).
More processing can increase usable information (data-processing inequality forbids it).

further_reading.title: Elements of Information Theory
further_reading.authors: Thomas M. Cover and Joy A. Thomas

further_reading.title: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms

topics.name: Algorithmic Information Theory and Minimum Description Length
topics.definition: Algorithmic information theory measures the complexity of an object by the length of the shortest program producing it; minimum description length operationalizes learning as compressing data plus model.
topics.explanation: Kolmogorov complexity K(x) is the length of the shortest program that outputs x; it is uncomputable but well-defined, invariant up to an additive constant across universal machines, and it redefines randomness as incompressibility (a sequence is random iff its prefixes have complexity close to their length). This reframes induction: the best explanation of data is the shortest program that generates it (Levin's universal prior weights hypotheses by 2^{-K}, an idealized Occam's razor that is provably within constants of any computable prior). Minimum description length makes a computable, practical version: the total code length of model plus data-given-model is minimized, yielding universal distributions from the normalized maximum likelihood (NML) and regret bounds that are minimax-optimal and prior-free, contrasting Bayesian priors with the frequentist worst-case guarantee that NML controls. MDL's two-part codes and the stochastic complexity formalize model selection, and its connections to structural risk minimization link compression to generalization. This topic supplies the deepest 'why simpler models generalize' argument and the formal limits of induction that pure likelihood cannot express.
learning_objectives: Define K(x) and explain invariance under a change of universal machine.
Characterize randomness via incompressibility of prefixes.
Explain Levin universal search and its optimality up to a constant.
Write a two-part MDL code and connect it to stochastic complexity.
Describe NML and the minimax regret it achieves.
common_misconceptions: Kolmogorov complexity is computable (it is not, by the halting problem).
MDL is exactly Bayesian (it is worst-case / regret based, not prior based).
A compressible model automatically generalizes (the risk bound must hold).

further_reading.title: An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications

subdomains.name: Discrete Mathematics, Logic and Graphs
subdomains.summary: The combinatorial, logical and spectral-graph structure that ML relies on, including why the model-theory / proof-theory connection is real rather than cosmetic.

topics.name: Spectral Graph Theory for Learning
topics.definition: Spectral graph theory relates a graph's combinatorial structure to the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of its adjacency and Laplacian matrices, yielding algebraic tools for clustering, embedding, and diffusion.
topics.explanation: Graphs encode relational data, and their algebra is the adjacency and (normalized) Laplacian matrices. The spectrum of the Laplacian reveals connectivity: the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue equals the number of connected components, the Fiedler vector (second eigenvector) gives an approximate balanced cut, and Cheeger's inequality ties the spectral gap to the graph conductance, so a small gap means a bottleneck. This is the mathematical engine of spectral clustering (Ng-Jordan-Weiss), which cuts the eigenvectors of a similarity graph to recover clusters that k-means cannot on non-convex shapes. Random walks and diffusion on graphs are governed by the same spectrum, motivating graph embeddings, graph signal processing (smoothing as a spectral filter), and the message-passing / permutation-invariance limits that explain what graph neural networks can and cannot express (they inherit the Weisfeiler-Lehman 1-test limitation). Combinatorial tools - Hall's theorem, matroids (the greedy-optimality structure behind matching and some feature selection), Ramsey-type results (structure vs randomness in large datasets), and generating functions - appear across discrete ML. The model-theory and proof-theory relevance is genuine: logical definability of graph properties (0-1 laws, Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse games) bounds what logical / message-passing programs can express, and proof complexity mirrors the difficulty of automating reasoning; a curriculum that omits these undersells what ML can represent.
learning_objectives: Form adjacency and Laplacian matrices and read connectivity from the spectrum.
State Cheeger's inequality and explain the Fiedler vector's cut.
Derive spectral clustering and relate it to graph Laplacian regularization.
Connect random-walk convergence to the spectral gap.
Explain the Weisfeiler-Lehman expressivity limit for message-passing GNNs.
common_misconceptions: The number of eigenvalues near zero reflects the number of good-quality clusters (zero-multiplicity counts true components).
Spectral clustering never needs a pre-specified number of clusters (it does; eigengap heuristics estimate it).
Message-passing GNNs can distinguish any two graphs (the WL-1 bound limits this).

topics.name: Logic, Probabilistic Reasoning and Knowledge Representation
topics.definition: Mathematical logic supplies the formal languages of reasoning (propositional, first-order), whose satisfiability, provability, and uncertainty structure underpin symbolic ML, logic programs, and probabilistic graphical reasoning.
topics.explanation: Machine learning increasingly hybridizes with reasoning: logical constraints in structured prediction, satisfiability solvers in neuro-symbolic models, and probabilistic logic in graphical models. Propositional and first-order logic supply definability and the compactness / completeness theorems; the boundary between decidable and undecidable fragments (with Godel's incompleteness) is what keeps automated reasoning honest about its limits. Resolution, DPLL/CDCL SAT solving, and answer-set programming are the algorithms; model theory (via Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse games and 0-1 laws) measures how expressive a formalism or a message-passing network can be, and proof complexity mirrors the hardness of inference, echoing the complexity topic elsewhere. On the uncertain side, de Finetti's representation theorem (exchangeability implies a mixture of i.i.d. sequences) grounds Bayesian nonparametrics and the very idea of a prior; probabilistic soft logic and Markov logic networks fuse weighted clauses with graphical models, and probabilistic programming compiles such declarations into inference. This topic is where 'discrete math and logic' stops being filler and becomes the formal scaffolding of reasoning-aware ML, and it deliberately references rather than duplicates the cross-area causal slugs.
learning_objectives: Distinguish propositional vs first-order expressiveness and give an ML example of each.
Explain completeness/compactness and the undecidable / decidable fragments.
Summarize SAT / resolution / answer-set programming and where they enter ML.
State de Finetti's exchangeability theorem and its Bayesian consequence.
Connect probabilistic logic / soft constraints to structured prediction.
common_misconceptions: Logical constraints and statistical models are incompatible (probabilistic logic unifies them).
Any expressible property is learnable/decidable (incompleteness and undecidable fragments limit this).
Exchangeable equals i.i.d. (it is a mixture of i.i.d., per de Finetti).

further_reading.title: An Introduction to Probabilistic Soft Logic
further_reading.authors: Stephen H. Bach, Matthias Broecheler, Bert Huang, Lise Getoor

subdomains.name: Dynamical Systems, Games and Control
subdomains.summary: Stability and iterative-dynamics analysis, game-theoretic equilibrium for learning, and optimal control / dynamic programming - the mathematics of processes that evolve and interact.

topics.name: Dynamical Systems, Stability and Optimal Control
topics.definition: Dynamical systems study the iterates of maps and flows; stability theory classifies attracting behavior; optimal control chooses inputs to steer a system while minimizing a cost, with dynamic programming as its recursion.
topics.explanation: Gradient descent, momentum, alternating minimization, and recurrent networks are all discrete dynamical systems, so their convergence is a stability question: fixed points correspond to stationary points of the loss, the eigenvalues of the Jacobian determine local attraction, and Lyapunov functions certify global behavior. Contraction analysis gives exponential forgetting of initial conditions, which justifies why a well-tuned optimizer forgets its start and is the right lens for analyzing momentum and mirror descent; bifurcation theory explains where an optimizer loses stability as the learning rate increases (period-doubling toward chaos at too-large steps), reframing the 'diverging loss' symptom as a dynamical phase transition. On the control side, linear systems with quadratic cost yield the LQR solution via the algebraic Riccati equation, controllability/observability (Kalman rank conditions) describe reachability, and Pontryagin's maximum principle and Bellman's dynamic programming give the general optimal policy as the fixed point of a value recursion. This is the same mathematics behind Kalman filtering (optimal linear state estimation) and reinforces the cross-area MDP / Bellman topics without redefining them, while adding the continuous-time and stability viewpoint they usually omit.
learning_objectives: Linearize an iterate map and read stability off its Jacobian eigenvalues.
Build a Lyapunov function to certify convergence of an optimizer.
Explain contraction analysis and its relevance to forgetting initialization.
Derive the LQR gain from the algebraic Riccati equation.
State the Bellman recursion and connect it to dynamic programming.
math_foundations: Fixed points and Jacobians of maps
common_misconceptions: A larger learning rate only slows convergence (it can destabilize via bifurcation).
Lyapunov stability requires the system to be linear.
LQR needs a costless unconstrained setting with no Riccati equation.

further_reading.title: Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers
further_reading.authors: Karl Johan Astrom and Richard M. Murray

topics.name: Game Theory for Machine Learning
topics.definition: Game theory studies strategic agents whose outcomes depend on joint actions, providing equilibrium concepts (Nash, minimax) and learning dynamics (no-regret) that model adversarial and multi-agent ML.
topics.explanation: Modern ML is replete with interacting optimizers: GANs pit a generator against a discriminator, reinforcement learning involves best responses in a multi-agent or sequential game, and robust/adversarial training is a min-max (or min-max-max) game between model and perturbation. Zero-sum games enjoy the von Neumann minimax theorem (the saddle-point value exists and pure strategies can be replaced by mixed ones), which is why a convex-concave objective like the GAN value has a solution concept and why the SVM / adversarial duals hold. General-sum games need Nash equilibrium, guaranteed to exist (Nash, via Kakutani fixed-point) but computationally hard (PPAD-complete) and often a poor predictor of learned outcomes. The bridge to learning is no-regret dynamics: if every player runs a regret-minimizing algorithm (multiplicative weights / Hedge, follow-the-regularized-leader, gradient descent-ascent), the empirical play converges to coarse-correlated / Nash equilibria, giving a learning-theoretic foundation for equilibrium rather than assuming it. Mean-field game theory scales this to many interacting agents, and regret bounds give the convergence story for training dynamics. This is the game-theoretic content most ML curricula leave out entirely.
learning_objectives: State the minimax theorem and apply it to a convex-concave GAN-like objective.
Define Nash equilibrium and explain its existence and computational hardness.
Derive multiplicative-weights and relate its regret bound to equilibrium convergence.
Explain gradient descent-ascent dynamics for zero-sum games.
Summarize mean-field games as the many-agent limit.
common_misconceptions: Nash equilibrium is easy to compute (it is PPAD-hard and can be bad).
GANs converge because they have a single fixed point (they can cycle; dynamics matter).
Zero-sum requires pure strategies (mixed strategies often dominate).

further_reading.title: Algorithmic Game Theory
further_reading.authors: Noam Nisan, Tim Roughgarden, Eva Tardos, Vijay V. Vazirani

subdomains.name: Computational Complexity and Statistical Learning Theory
subdomains.summary: What is efficiently computable and learnable: P/NP and average-case hardness, sample and query complexity, and the VC / Rademacher / PAC-Bayes / minimax framework with No-Free-Lunch limits.

topics.name: Computational Complexity and Hardness of Learning
topics.definition: Computational complexity classifies problems by their intrinsic resource requirements; hardness of learning identifies which concept classes cannot be learned efficiently under standard cryptographic / complexity assumptions.
topics.explanation: Generalization theory asks what is statistically learnable; complexity asks what is efficiently computable, and the two interact sharply. The classes P, NP, and coNP, Cook-Levin reductions and NP-completeness (3-SAT, clique) explain why many exact ML problems (optimal decision trees, subset selection, MAP inference in general graphical models, k-means with arbitrary k) are NP-hard and why heuristics dominate. Average-case hardness and one-way functions - problems easy to compute but hard to invert - are the realistic basis for cryptographic lower bounds and for hardness of learning: Kearns-Vazirani style results reduce learning certain classes to factoring or breaking pseudorandomness, so 'efficiently learnable' has teeth only when the underlying distribution is not adversarial. Circuit lower bounds and the PAC model's computational refinement (which concept classes are efficiently PAC-learnable) explain, for example, why learning linear separators is efficient but learning intersections of halfspaces is not. This topic complements the cross-area computational-complexity slug by focusing on the learning consequences and links directly to the hardness-of-inference results in graphical models.
learning_objectives: Explain NP-completeness via Cook-Levin and give a reduction from 3-SAT to an ML problem.
Distinguish statistical learnability from computational tractability.
State the Kearns-Vazirani flavor: learning is hard because inversion / cryptography is hard.
Explain why exact MAP inference is NP-hard and approximate methods are used.
Relate average-case vs worst-case hardness to realistic training.
applications: Why exact trees / MAP / subset selection are heuristic
Complexity of inference in graphical models
common_misconceptions: Anything statistically learnable is efficiently learnable (complexity can block it).
NP-hard means every instance is hard (worst-case only; average case may be easy).
Heuristics disprove complexity results.

further_reading.title: An Introduction to Computational Learning Theory
further_reading.authors: Michael J. Kearns and Umesh V. Vazirani

topics.name: Statistical Learning Theory: VC, Rademacher and Generalization
topics.definition: Statistical learning theory bounds the gap between empirical risk on training data and true risk on the distribution, using complexity measures such as VC dimension and Rademacher complexity, and proves what sample size suffices for learning.
topics.explanation: The central fact: a learner that fits training data well generalizes only if its hypothesis class is not too rich. Empirical risk minimization replaces the unknown true risk with the sample average, and uniform convergence (the supremum of the risk gap over the class tending to zero) is what justifies it. The combinatorial dimension that controls this is the Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension - the largest set the class can shatter - with the Sauer-Shelah lemma linking shattering to growth functions. Rademacher complexity refines this: the expected correlation of the class with random +/- signs measures its capacity directly and yields sharper, model-specific bounds, and Dudley's entropy integral bounds it via metric entropy, connecting to the high-dimensional-probability topic. Minimax-optimal rates show some classes are fundamentally learnable only at a given speed, and the PAC framework quantifies confidence-vs-sample-size trade-offs. Algorithmic stability and compression-based bounds give further guarantees. The most honest caveat: generalization bounds are famously loose for deep networks; the PAC-Bayes and No-Free-Lunch topic completes this picture by giving posterior-based bounds and fundamental limits.
learning_objectives: Define shattering and VC dimension; compute VC dimension of halfspaces.
State the Sauer-Shelah lemma and its consequence for growth functions.
Bound expected generalization error via Rademacher complexity.
Derive a sample-complexity bound from uniform convergence.
Explain why these bounds are loose for deep networks.
common_misconceptions: A model with high training capacity must overfit (capacity controls a bound, not a guarantee of overfit).
Classical generalization bounds explain deep-network behavior (they are largely vacuous there).
VC dimension counts parameters (it is a combinatorial count of shattering).

further_reading.title: Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms
Foundations of Machine Learning
further_reading.authors: Mehry Mohri, Afshin Rostamizadeh, Ameet Talwalkar

topics.name: Minimax Rates, No-Free-Lunch and PAC-Bayes
topics.definition: Minimax rates give the optimal worst-case sample complexity of a learning problem; No-Free-Lunch says no learner beats random guessing averaged over all distributions; PAC-Bayes bounds generalization of stochastic predictors via a prior-posterior KL term.
topics.explanation: Upper bounds from generalization theory tell you a learner can do this well; minimax lower bounds tell you no learner can do fundamentally better, and matching them defines the true difficulty of a problem (e.g., nonparametric regression rates d/(2s+d) for s-smooth functions in d dimensions, or parametric 1/n). Lower bounds are proved with the same Le Cam / Fano machinery as decision theory, so the rate is a property of the model class, not the algorithm. The No-Free-Lunch theorem (Wolpert, and the Shalev-Shwartz Ben-David learning-theoretic version) is the sobering meta-result: averaged uniformly over all possible data distributions, every learner has the same risk as guessing; the value of a good inductive bias is precisely that it restricts the class to a subset where a learner can win, which ties generalization directly to the choice of hypothesis class. PAC-Bayes bounds (McAllester, Catoni) are the most flexible generalization tool: they control the expected risk of a distribution over hypotheses by an empirical risk plus KL(posterior || prior)/n, giving non-vacuous bounds for deep networks when the prior is data-dependent or the posterior is noisy, and connecting to information-theoretic generalization and compression arguments. Together these three concepts form the 'what is and is not learnable, and how fast' layer.
learning_objectives: Prove a matching minimax upper/lower bound for a simple model class.
State No-Free-Lunch and explain what inductive bias buys.
Derive a basic PAC-Bayes bound from a Chernoff / change-of-measure argument.
Explain why PAC-Bayes gives a 1/n KL term and a non-vacuous deep-net bound.
Relate smoothness to a nonparametric minimax rate.
common_misconceptions: A clever algorithm can beat NFL on the uniform-over-all-distributions average (it cannot).
Minimax lower bounds depend on the algorithm (they bound any algorithm).
PAC-Bayes is always vacuous (data-dependent priors and noise make it non-vacuous).

Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep (Stochastic) Neural Networks with Many More Parameters than Training Data

subdomains.name: Functional Analysis and Harmonic Analysis
subdomains.summary: Infinite-dimensional linear structure - Hilbert spaces and reproducing kernels - plus Fourier analysis, the frequency lens on learning.

topics.name: Functional Analysis and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
topics.definition: Functional analysis studies infinite-dimensional vector spaces with norms and inner products; a reproducing kernel Hilbert space is one in which point evaluation is continuous, so a kernel encodes the geometry.
topics.explanation: Learning a function is inherently infinite-dimensional, so the right setting is Hilbert and Banach spaces rather than R^d. The core results are the projection theorem (best approximation onto a closed convex set), the Riesz representation theorem (every bounded linear functional is an inner product with a unique representer), and completeness, which guarantees limits of Cauchy sequences of hypotheses exist. A reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) is a Hilbert space of functions where evaluation at a point is a bounded functional, so Riesz gives a kernel function k(x, .) that reproduces f(x) = <f, k(x, .)>. The Moore-Aronszajn theorem says every positive-definite kernel defines a unique RKHS, which is the rigorous basis of the kernel trick: SVMs, kernel ridge regression, and Gaussian processes all optimize over an implicit infinite-dimensional feature space using only the finite Gram matrix. Mercer's theorem characterizes when a continuous symmetric kernel on a compact domain admits an eigenfunction expansion with a countable feature map, giving the spectral view of kernels and the link to kernel PCA and integral operators. Norm constraints in an RKHS are the natural 'smoothness' regularizer, and the representer theorem reduces an infinite-dimensional variational problem to a finite one spanned by the training points, which is why kernel methods are computable. This is the mathematics underpinning the kernel-methods classical topic, stated in functional-analytic terms.
learning_objectives: State the projection and Riesz theorems and apply them to function approximation.
Define an RKHS and verify the reproducing property from a kernel.
Use the Moore-Aronszajn theorem to construct an RKHS from a positive-definite kernel.
State Mercer's theorem and expand a kernel into its eigenfunctions.
Derive the representer theorem reducing RKHS minimization to a Gram matrix.
math_foundations: Inner products and norms on function spaces
common_misconceptions: A kernel is just a similarity score (it must be positive-definite to define an RKHS).
The feature map of an RKHS is always finite-dimensional (it can be countably/infinite).
The representer theorem holds for any loss and regularizer (needs a pointwise loss and RKHS-norm penalty).

further_reading.authors: Bernhard Scholkopf and Alexander J. J. Smola

further_reading.title: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces in Probability and Statistics

topics.name: Fourier Analysis for Machine Learning
topics.definition: Fourier analysis decomposes functions into sinusoidal / character modes, turning convolution into multiplication and making a function's frequency content explicit.
topics.explanation: Many ML operators are translations or convolutions (layers in convolutional networks, kernels, attention weightings), and the Fourier transform diagonalizes convolution, turning it into pointwise multiplication; this is why FFT-based convolution is fast and why equivariant and translation-invariant architectures have a natural frequency interpretation. The spectral view also explains phenomena that look mysterious in the spatial domain: the bias of networks toward low frequencies and the 'spectral bias' of gradient descent (Neural Tangent Kernel analysis) explains why networks fit smooth patterns first; periodic positional encodings in transformers are literally Fourier features, and random Fourier features (Rahimi-Recht) approximate shift-invariant kernels by explicit sinusoidal maps, making kernel methods scale linearly. Convergence of Fourier series, the sampling / Nyquist theorem, and Parseval / energy conservation are the classical underpinnings; wavelets and multi-resolution bases refine this for localized, non-stationary signals. The uncertainty principle (a function and its Fourier transform cannot both be sharply localized) recurs as the time-frequency trade-off in signal and audio ML. A learner fluent in the Fourier lens reads kernels, convnets, positional encodings, and spectral regularization as the same idea viewed in the right basis.
learning_objectives: Use the convolution theorem to replace a convolution by pointwise multiplication.
Explain the Nyquist / sampling theorem and aliasing.
Derive random Fourier features approximating a shift-invariant kernel.
Relate spectral bias / the NTK to the frequency content a network learns.
Connect positional encodings to a Fourier basis.
common_misconceptions: A network learns all frequencies equally fast (low frequencies dominate early).
Convolution in the Fourier domain requires re-solving (it becomes multiplication).
Random Fourier features are exact (they are an unbiased approximation).

subdomains.name: Geometry, Topology and Random Matrix Theory
subdomains.summary: Spectral laws of large random matrices, the differential and information geometry of model families, and the topology of data via persistent homology.

topics.name: Random Matrix Theory for Machine Learning
topics.definition: Random matrix theory describes the bulk spectrum and edge eigenvalues of large matrices with random entries, yielding universal laws that predict the behavior of covariances, initializations, and Hessians.
topics.explanation: As dimensions grow, individual eigenvalues are less important than the distribution of eigenvalues, and random matrix theory gives it exactly. The Wigner semicircle law describes the bulk eigenvalues of a symmetric random matrix; the Marchenko-Pastur law governs the eigenvalues of a sample covariance matrix as dimension and sample size grow proportionally, and it is the reason sample covariance is a biased estimate of true covariance and why spurious eigenvalues appear. The BBP phase transition determines when an injected signal eigenvalue emerges from the random bulk, which is the basis of PCA denoising and signal detection: you should trust eigenvalues above the bulk edge and distrust those inside it. Free probability provides a calculus for non-commuting random matrices, predicting the spectral convolution of products and sums, which underlies the analysis of random initializations and the loss-surface spectra of neural networks. Practically, RMT is how a learner diagnoses overfitting in high dimensions, chooses how many principal components to keep against the noise floor, and understands the Hessian / Fisher / Jacobian spectra behind optimization difficulty. This topic makes the high-dimensional-probability and learning-theory bounds concrete by giving the actual asymptotic spectra.
learning_objectives: State the Wigner semicircle and Marchenko-Pastur laws and their conditions.
Use the BBP threshold to decide which PCA components exceed the noise floor.
Explain the bias of a sample covariance in high dimensions via Marchenko-Pastur.
Apply a free-probability convolution to a product of random matrices.
Connect Hessian / Jacobian spectra to optimization behavior.
common_misconceptions: All large eigenvalues of a sample covariance are signal (the bulk is noise; use the MP edge).
Sample covariance eigenvalues equal true covariance eigenvalues (they spread systematically).
RMT is only about physics and irrelevant to data (it directly governs ML spectra).
