further_reading.title: Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability

topics.name: Differential Geometry and Information Geometry
topics.definition: Differential geometry treats parameter spaces as curved manifolds with metrics and geodesics; information geometry equips a family of probability distributions with the Fisher metric and a dual pair of flat connections.
topics.explanation: A statistical model is a manifold: the set of distributions parameterized smoothly, and Euclidean intuition misleads because parameters are not intrinsically meaningful. The Fisher information matrix is the natural Riemannian metric on this manifold, measuring how much a small parameter change moves the distribution (KL divergence to second order equals half the Fisher quadratic form), and geodesics under this metric give the shortest paths between distributions. Amari's information geometry reveals that exponential families carry a dual pair of flat (e) and (m) connections whose divergence is a Bregman divergence, yielding an Euclidean-like duality structure. This is precisely the geometry behind natural gradient descent: because plain gradient descent depends on the (arbitrary) parameterization while the Fisher-metric-rescaled gradient is invariant, natural gradient follows a geodesic-like update on the statistical manifold, which improves optimization for poorly-conditioned and high-curvature problems and explains why preconditioning by the Fisher or its empirical estimator is effective. The geometry of optimal transport (Wasserstein) provides an alternative metric on distributions; curvature (information curvature) flags genuinely non-Euclidean families such as Gaussian scale families, not merely curved coordinates. This topic unifies the natural-gradient and divergence ideas seen elsewhere into one coherent geometric language.
learning_objectives: Define the Fisher metric and derive it as the second-order KL expansion.
Explain e/m dual connections and Bregman-divergence duality for exponential families.
Derive natural gradient from the Fisher metric and argue parameterization invariance.
Distinguish intrinsic curvature from mere coordinate curvature.
Relate Wasserstein and Fisher/Riemannian geometries of distributions.
common_misconceptions: Natural gradient is just Adam (it rescales by the Fisher metric, not by squared gradients).
All parameterizations give the same geometry (the Fisher metric is invariant; Euclidean is not).
Fisher equals Hessian in general (equal only at the MLE / for well-specified likelihoods).

topics.name: Topological Data Analysis and Persistent Homology
topics.definition: Topological data analysis infers the shape of data by building simplicial complexes at many scales and tracking which topological features persist; persistent homology encodes these features as barcodes or diagrams.
topics.explanation: Classical statistics has no language for the 'shape' of a point cloud, but topology does: connected components (0D), loops/cycles (1D), and voids (2D) are detected by homology. Given data one builds a filtration of simplicial complexes (Vietoris-Rips or Cech) parameterized by a distance threshold, so as the threshold grows features appear (birth) and disappear (death); persistent homology records the birth-death pair of each feature as a bar in a barcode or a point in a persistence diagram. Features that persist across many scales are treated as signal, while short-lived ones are noise - a principled denoising criterion invariant to the choice of coordinates. The algebraic stability theorem guarantees persistence diagrams change by at most the Hausdorff perturbation of the input, so persistent features are robust and differentiable-approximable (persistent-homology layers exist). Practical ML uses are more than decoration: topology-aware loss functions that penalize wrong homology (e.g., ensuring segmented images have the right number of loops), topological features for classification (persistent landscapes / images vectorized into a learning model), Mapper as a multiscale clustering/reduction tool, and characterizing the topology of loss landscapes and generated-manifold coverage. It is a niche but genuine frontier, and the reason an 'AI-from-foundations' curriculum should name it rather than omit it.
learning_objectives: Build a Vietoris-Rips filtration from point-cloud data.
Define homology groups and explain Betti numbers as feature counts.
Read a persistence diagram and separate persistent features from noise.
State the algebraic stability theorem for persistence.
Vectorize a persistence diagram into a feature (persistence landscape/image).
common_misconceptions: TDA replaces standard features in most pipelines (it is currently niche; benefits are shape-specific).
Long bars are noise (they are signal; short bars are noise).
Persistence diagrams are unique up to arbitrary matching (the bottleneck distance defines their metric).

further_reading.title: Computational Topology: An Introduction
further_reading.authors: Herbert Edelsbrunner and John L. Harer

subdomains.name: Approximation Theory and Numerical Methods
subdomains.summary: The mathematics of how well function classes approximate targets, plus the numerical methods for PDEs, integration, and sampling that make continuous models computable.

topics.name: Approximation Theory for Machine Learning
topics.definition: Approximation theory quantifies how well a target function can be represented by a restricted class (polynomials, splines, wavelets, networks) and how the error depends on the class's capacity.
topics.explanation: Every model is a claim that a target function lies near some tractable class, and approximation theory is the mathematics of 'near'. The Weierstrass theorem guarantees polynomials are dense in continuous functions on a compact interval, while Jackson's theorem gives the quantitative rate: approximation error by degree-n polynomials decays like the function's modulus of smoothness, so smoother targets are approximated faster. Bernstein operators give a constructive proof that doubles as an early approximation argument, and Kolmogorov n-widths measure how well an entire function class (say s-smooth unit balls) can be approximated by any n-dimensional subspace - directly connecting to optimal feature-dimension selection and the minimax rates in learning theory. Splines and wavelets provide multi-resolution bases whose approximation power depends on the target's spatial regularity, and the best-n-term view of sparsity explains why a few well-chosen basis functions beat dense representations. The universal approximation theorem for neural networks (Cybenko, Hornik) is an existence result that a bounded continuous function can be approximated arbitrarily well by a single-hidden-layer network; the crucial caveat is that it says nothing about size, learnability, or rate - the rates, not the density, are what approximation theory supplies. This is the bridge between 'can it represent' and 'how well at what cost'.
learning_objectives: State the Weierstrass and Jackson theorems and relate error to smoothness.
Define Kolmogorov n-width and its role in feature-dimension choice.
Explain the universal approximation theorem's meaning and its limits.
Compare polynomial, spline, and wavelet approximation for a target.
Relate best n-term approximation to sparse representation.
common_misconceptions: Universal approximation means nets learn any function fast (it says nothing about rates or optimization).
More parameters always reduce approximation error (bias-variance / width trade-off applies).
Approximation and estimation are the same (approximation is the bias floor before sampling).

further_reading.title: Multilayer Feedforward Networks Are Universal Approximators
further_reading.authors: Kurt Hornik, Maxwell Stinchcombe, Halbert White

topics.name: Numerical Methods for PDEs, Quadrature and Sampling
topics.definition: These are the computational tools for continuous problems: discretizing differential equations, approximating high-dimensional integrals (quadrature), and drawing representative samples when analytic integration is impossible.
topics.explanation: Many ML objectives and models are continuous: partition functions, Bayesian evidence, expected losses, diffusion and Fokker-Planck forward/backward equations, and physics-informed constraints are all integrals or PDEs that must be solved numerically. For ODE/PDEs, finite-difference and finite-element discretizations convert operators into matrices; stability and accuracy trade off through the CFL condition and consistency/stability (Lax equivalence) analysis, and spectral methods give exponential convergence for smooth periodic problems. For integrals, classical quadrature (Newton-Cotes, Gaussian quadrature) is effective in low dimension but suffers the curse of dimensionality; Monte Carlo integration estimates the integral by the average of sampled function values with an O(1/sqrt(n)) dimension-independent error, which is why sampling-based estimation dominates in high dimensions. Quasi-Monte Carlo (low-discrepancy Sobol / Halton sequences), stratified sampling, and Latin hypercube sampling reduce variance below plain MC by spreading coverage, and importance sampling reweights toward the region where the integrand is concentrated (basis of self-normalized importance sampling and of the variational-inference topic). These methods are also how a diffusion model's score / SDE is integrated and how intractable normalizing constants are estimated. This topic grounds the sampling/quadrature ideas used throughout generative modeling and probabilistic inference, complementing the cross-area Monte Carlo slugs with the deterministic-continuous side.
learning_objectives: Discretize a PDE with finite differences / elements and discuss stability (CFL).
Estimate a high-dimensional integral by Monte Carlo and bound its error.
Construct importance sampling and explain the self-normalized variant.
Compare quasi-MC, stratified, and Latin-hypercube sampling for variance reduction.
Relate quadrature accuracy to the curse of dimensionality.
math_foundations: Expected value and variance of estimators
Numerical linear algebra for sparse systems
common_misconceptions: Gaussian quadrature scales to high dimensions (it degrades via the curse of dimensionality).
Monte Carlo error improves at a dimension-independent exponential rate (it is 1/sqrt(n)).
Importance sampling can use any proposal (heavy-tailed proposals blow up variance).

further_reading.authors: Christian P. Robert and George Casella

domains.name: Foundations of Machine Learning
domains.summary: The problem formulations and learning regimes that sit between raw mathematics and concrete algorithms: what it means to learn a mapping, to discover structure without labels, and to operate when labels are scarce, the distribution moves, the stream never stops, or the data cannot leave its owner. This domain names the paradigms that a lesson author chooses from before implementing a model, and it makes explicit the assumptions (i.i.d. sampling, clean balanced labels, a single fixed task) that classical algorithms silently rely on and that deployment routinely breaks.

subdomains.name: Learning Paradigms
subdomains.summary: The supervised and unsupervised problem settings, and the intermediate regimes that stretch a labelled budget through semi-, self- and representation learning.

topics.name: Supervised Learning Foundations
topics.definition: Supervised learning estimates a mapping from inputs to targets by minimizing a loss over labelled examples, trading fidelity to the training set against model complexity so that the fitted rule generalises to unseen data.
topics.explanation: The organising idea is empirical risk minimisation: replace the unknown population risk with an average over observed pairs and select, from a hypothesis class, the function that best fits the data under a chosen loss. Everything that follows is a negotiation between that fit and the capacity of the class, made precise by the bias-variance decomposition and by the generalisation bounds studied in statistical learning theory. The choice of loss (squared, absolute, hinge, cross-entropy) encodes the assumed conditional model and dictates robustness and gradient behaviour, so loss engineering is a modelling decision, not a detail. Classification and regression share the framework but differ sharply in evaluation: accuracy is misleading under imbalance, and precision/recall, F1, Matthews correlation and ROC/PR analysis carry the real information. Generative methods model the joint P(X,Y) and obtain P(Y|X) by Bayes, while discriminative methods model the conditional directly; the comparison explains many practical gaps. A competent practitioner must be able to state the objective, name the inductive bias, detect label leakage, and read a test curve without confusing optimisation success with generalisation.
learning_objectives: Write the empirical and population risk for a given loss and hypothesis class.
Derive the bias-variance decomposition and explain how model capacity moves each term.
Choose an appropriate loss and evaluation metric for a balanced or imbalanced task.
Distinguish generative from discriminative modelling and give one example of each.
Identify label leakage and data-snooping in an experimental setup.
math_foundations: Empirical risk as a sample average over n pairs
Convexity and differentiability of common losses
common_misconceptions: Low training loss implies low test loss (overfitting is the whole difficulty).
Accuracy is adequate under severe class imbalance (prefer precision/recall, F1, MCC).
Discriminative and generative models estimate the same quantity by the same route.

further_reading.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning
further_reading.authors: Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, Jerome Friedman

further_reading.title: Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms

topics.name: Unsupervised Learning Foundations
topics.definition: Unsupervised learning models structure in unlabelled data, grouping, reducing dimension, estimating density, or discovering latent factors, seeking a compressed or generative description of the inputs in the absence of any target signal.
topics.explanation: With no labels there is no external reward, so an unsupervised method is defined by the objective it optimises, and different objectives, reconstruction error, log-likelihood, separation, graph smoothness, expose different, none uniquely correct, structure. This is the identifiability problem: latent-variable models are recoverable only up to the symmetry of their assumptions, so the practitioner must state which inductive bias licenses the interpretation. The field splits into clustering (assign discrete groupings), dimensionality reduction (find a low-dimensional representation), density estimation (model p(x)) and latent-factor/generative modelling (model how data arise), all of which concrete classical algorithms realise. Evaluation is correspondingly delicate: internal indices such as silhouette or Davies-Bouldin score geometry, external indices such as adjusted Rand or mutual information need hidden labels, and stability analysis probes sensitivity to resampling. Because a single dataset supports many defensible decompositions, unsupervised learning is as much about choosing the right question as the right algorithm. It underpins exploration, representation pretraining and anomaly detection, which is why the paradigms in this domain are introduced before the algorithms that implement them.
learning_objectives: Classify an unsupervised problem as clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation or latent-factor modelling.
Explain why latent-variable identifiability depends on distributional assumptions.
Compare internal, external and stability-based evaluation and when each is admissible.
Connect the optimisation objective of a method to the structure it is licensed to reveal.
key_results_or_algorithms: Adjusted Rand and normalized mutual information
math_foundations: Latent-variable marginalisation p(x) = integral p(x|z)p(z) dz
No unique ground-truth partition exists for raw data
common_misconceptions: Unsupervised learning needs no assumptions (identifiability requires them).
A clustering is the single correct partition (it is objective- and scale-dependent).
A high internal validity index certifies that the clusters are meaningful.

further_reading.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning
further_reading.authors: Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, Jerome Friedman

topics.name: Semi-Supervised, Self-Supervised and Representation Learning
topics.definition: This family stretches a limited labelling budget by propagating labels through unlabelled data (semi-supervised), manufacturing supervision from input transformations or context (self-supervised), and learning reusable feature maps whose geometry encodes similarity (representation and metric learning).
topics.explanation: Semi-supervised methods assume that unlabelled samples reveal the input geometry that labels alone cannot, exploiting the cluster, low-density-separation and manifold assumptions through self-training, co-training, consistency regularisation and graph label propagation; weak supervision generalises this by aggregating noisy labelling functions rather than trusting ground-truth labels, and positive-unlabeled learning handles the frequent case where only positives and a raw pool are available. Self-supervision removes the human label entirely by defining a pretext task, contrasting augmented views of the same item, predicting masked context, or reconstructing an input, so that the encoder learns features that transfer to downstream tasks; metric learning then shapes the embedding space directly with contrastive, triplet and siamese losses so that similarity, not class identity, is the geometric primitive. These regimes meet at representation learning, where the goal is not a prediction but a reusable embedding, with disentanglement as the strongest version. The shared subtlety is that every pretext or pseudo-label is an implicit, possibly biased, supervision signal, so confirmation effects and distribution mismatch are first-order concerns rather than footnotes.
learning_objectives: State the cluster, low-density and manifold assumptions that justify semi-supervised learning.
Contrast pseudo-labeling, consistency regularisation and weak-supervision aggregation.
Derive a contrastive InfoNCE objective and relate it to mutual-information estimation.
Design a metric-learning loss and explain its sensitivity to sampling of pairs/triplets.
Evaluate whether a learned representation transfers, not merely whether it reconstructs.
math_foundations: InfoNCE as a lower bound on mutual information
common_misconceptions: Pseudo-labels are always safe (they entrench early mistakes).
Self-supervision is genuinely label-free (pretext tasks are implicit, biased labels).
More unlabelled data necessarily improves the model (distribution mismatch can hurt).

A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations
further_reading.authors: Ting Chen, Simon Kornblith, Mohammad Norouzi, Geoffrey Hinton

further_reading.authors: Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, Aaron Courville

subdomains.name: Adaptivity, Continuity and Data Robustness
subdomains.summary: Learning under shifting tasks, streaming data, expensive labels, and corrupted or unevenly distributed training conditions.

topics.name: Transfer, Online, Active and Continual Learning
topics.definition: These paradigms adapt a learner to changing task budgets and data: transferring source knowledge to a label-poor target, updating sequentially with per-round guarantees, querying the most informative labels under budget, and accumulating tasks without erasing earlier ones.
topics.explanation: Transfer learning and domain adaptation refuse the assumption that training and test data are identically distributed, reusing a source model through fine-tuning, feature reuse, or alignment of source and target via importance weighting, discrepancy measures such as Wasserstein distances, or adversarial adaptation; domain generalisation and few/zero-shot and meta-learning push this further by learning from a distribution of tasks so the model rapidly acquires new ones, with model-agnostic meta-learning as the canonical gradient-based formulation. Online learning abandons the batch setting entirely, replacing risk with cumulative regret against the best fixed competitor, which connects the field to game theory and no-regret dynamics and makes streaming SGD a principled algorithm rather than an approximation hack. Active learning treats labels as costly and asks which unlabelled point to acquire, using uncertainty, expected-model-change or coverage criteria to shrink the needed sample. Continual/lifelong learning adds a sequence of tasks and the twin hazards of catastrophic forgetting and task interference, addressed by regularisation (elastic weight consolidation), replay and dynamic architectures; curriculum learning orders examples or tasks to ease optimisation. The unifying lesson is that budgets, streams and task shifts change what an optimum even means, so guarantees must be restated per regime.
learning_objectives: Distinguish transfer learning, domain adaptation, domain generalisation and meta-learning.
State a regret bound for an online convex optimisation algorithm and interpret it.
Derive a query-by-uncertainty acquisition rule and name its failure modes.
Explain catastrophic forgetting and compare regularisation, replay and architectural remedies.
Relate online-to-batch conversion to classical generalisation guarantees.
common_misconceptions: Transfer always helps (negative transfer is common when domains conflict).
Online regret guarantees imply statistical generalisation for free (online-to-batch conversion has conditions).
Catastrophic forgetting is a solved problem (it remains open for general streams).

further_reading.title: A Survey on Transfer Learning
further_reading.authors: Sinno Jialin Pan and Qiang Yang

further_reading.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks

topics.name: Dataset Shift, Noisy Labels, Imbalance and Federated Learning
topics.definition: This topic groups the deployment-time violations of the clean, balanced, independent-and-identically-distributed training assumption: covariate, prior and concept shift with out-of-distribution detection, learning from corrupted labels, decisions under extreme class imbalance, and training when data never leave its owner (federated learning).
topics.explanation: Dataset shift is classified by what changes between train and test: the input marginal (covariate shift), the label marginal (prior shift), or the conditional itself (concept shift); each admits a different correction, importance weighting for covariate shift, black-box prior-shift correction for label shift, and retraining or drift detection for concept shift, with calibration and out-of-distribution scoring as the deployment guardrails. Label noise, whether class-conditional or instance-dependent, biases empirical risk away from true risk, and the robust response is loss-level, from symmetric/proxy losses and generalized cross-entropy to co-teaching and sample reweighting. Class imbalance turns the default accuracy metric into a lie and reframes the decision problem as cost-sensitive or threshold-tuned inference, handled by resampling, focal and weighted losses and by metrics such as balanced accuracy, precision-recall and Matthews correlation. Federated and distributed learning changes the data regime at the system level: optimisation must be communication-efficient (federated averaging), robust to non-IID client distributions and stragglers, and privacy-preserving, where differential-privacy accounting and the information-theoretic limits of noisy aggregates bound what a released model can reveal. These are the concrete places where the idealised objectives of statistical learning theory meet real data, and the same decision-theoretic and concentration tools from the mathematics domain supply the guarantees.
learning_objectives: Categorise a train/test mismatch as covariate, prior or concept shift and choose the matching correction.
Explain why accuracy fails under imbalance and select an appropriate metric and loss.
Describe how label noise shifts empirical risk and apply a robust loss or reweighting scheme.
State the federated averaging update and the non-IID and communication challenges it faces.
Relate differential-privacy accounting to information-theoretic leakage bounds.
math_foundations: Density ratio p_test(x)/p_train(x) for covariate shift
Confusion matrix and class priors under imbalance
common_misconceptions: Accuracy is a sufficient metric under extreme imbalance.
Covariate shift changes the conditional P(Y|X) (it does not, by definition).
Label noise is harmless to well-regularised learners (it biases the risk itself).

further_reading.authors: Zhi-Hua Zhang and Mehmet Egeer Sabuncu

domains.name: Classical Machine Learning
domains.summary: The model families and modelling workflow that predate deep learning and still dominate tabular, statistical and small-data practice: linear and generalised models, trees and their ensembles, kernel machines and Gaussian processes, instance-based and unsupervised structure learning, graphical models with their exact and approximate inference, and the disciplined engineering of features, validation and interpretation. Each topic aggregates a cluster of closely related algorithms the way standard references (ESL, PRML, PML) organise chapters, so lesson authors have one rich target per coherent method rather than a pile of stubs.

subdomains.name: Parametric, Linear and Kernel Models
subdomains.summary: Models whose prediction is a linear predictor, a likelihood from an exponential family, or a function recovered through inner products in a kernel feature space.

topics.name: Linear Models, Generalized Linear Models and Naive Bayes
topics.definition: The linear family expresses a target as a weighted combination of features: ordinary least squares and its regularised variants fit continuous responses, generalized linear models attach a link function and an exponential-family noise model to a linear predictor, and naive Bayes is a generative counterpart built from class-conditional densities.
topics.explanation: Ordinary least squares is the projection of the response onto the column space of the design matrix, solved by the normal equations, and under spherical errors Gauss-Markov makes it the best linear unbiased estimator; almost every regression difficulty is a modification of this picture. Regularisation adds a penalty to control variance and capacity: the L2 (ridge/Tikhonov) penalty shrinks coefficients smoothly and is stable under collinearity, the L1 (lasso) penalty produces exact zeros and hence sparsity through a soft-thresholding/subgradient geometry, and elastic net blends both for correlated predictors. Logistic regression is a generalized linear model with a Bernoulli noise term and the logit link, fit by maximising the conditional likelihood with iteratively reweighted least squares or convex first-order methods, and the GLM template extends this to count, positive and bounded outcomes via the canonical exponential family and link. Naive Bayes instead models the joint P(X,Y) with a class-conditional independence assumption, learns parameters by counting with smoothing, and recovers P(Y|X) through Bayes; it is frequently competitive with logistic regression despite a wrong independence prior, illustrating the generative-versus-discriminative distinction. Gaussian linear discriminant analysis and its quadratic variant round out the set of generative classifiers under Gaussian class-conditionals.
learning_objectives: Derive the normal equations and interpret least squares as an orthogonal projection.
State Gauss-Markov and its assumptions precisely.
Contrast ridge and lasso geometry and explain why L1 induces sparsity.
Write the logistic-regression likelihood and the iteratively reweighted least-squares update.
State the naive Bayes conditional independence assumption and the effect of Laplace smoothing.
Compare a generative and a discriminative classifier on the same task.
math_foundations: Normal equations (X^T X) beta = X^T y
Exponential-family form p(y|x) = exp(eta(x) T(y) - A(x))
L1-ball corner geometry producing sparse optima
common_misconceptions: Lasso is ridge with a different norm (it yields exact zeros and unstable selection among correlated features).
Logistic regression assumes a linear boundary in the raw features (it is linear in whatever features you supply).
Naive Bayes needs the independence assumption to hold to work well (it often performs strongly when violated).

further_reading.authors: Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani

topics.name: Support Vector Machines and Kernel Methods
topics.definition: Support vector machines find the maximum-margin separating hyperplane by solving a convex dual problem whose solution depends on the data only through inner products, so a kernel can replace the inner product and yield nonlinear decision boundaries living in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.
topics.explanation: The hard-margin SVM is a quadratic program; relaxing it with slack variables and a cost parameter C yields the soft-margin form that is exactly hinge loss with L2 regularisation, tying SVMs to the regularised-ERM view. Lagrangian duality and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions show that the solution is a sparse combination of support vectors and depends on inputs only via pairwise inner products, which is the kernel trick. Replacing inner products by a positive-definite kernel (linear, polynomial, radial-basis, spline) evaluates the learner in an implicit feature space, made rigorous by Mercer's theorem and the RKHS framework: the representer theorem proves the regularised optimum lies in the span of the training features, collapsing an infinite-dimensional problem to a finite one. Kernel ridge regression and support vector regression extend the same machinery to real-valued targets, and the SVM margin output is not a probability, requiring post-hoc calibration such as Platt scaling. Because exact kernel methods cost O(n^2) memory and O(n^3) time, scalable variants use reduced/support-set machines, Nyström approximation and random Fourier features, which connect kernel methods to the low-dimensional spectral view of deep networks. The result is a principled, convex, capacity-controlled nonparametric learner whose inductive bias is written directly as a kernel.
learning_objectives: Formulate soft-margin SVM as hinge loss with L2 regularisation.
Derive the SVM dual and explain why the solution is sparse in support vectors.
State Mercer's theorem and construct valid positive-definite kernels.
Explain the representer theorem and its role in reducing RKHS problems to finite dimension.
Describe kernel ridge regression and support vector regression.
Name scalable kernel approximations such as Nyström and random features.
math_foundations: Lagrangian duality and the KKT conditions
RKHS norm regularisation and the representer theorem
common_misconceptions: SVM output is a class probability (it is a margin; calibrate to get probabilities).
A larger C is always better (it lowers margin slack and can overfit).
Kernel methods need explicit feature maps (the kernel trick evaluates inner products without them).

further_reading.title: Learning with Kernels: Support Vector Machines, Regularization, Optimization, and Beyond
further_reading.authors: Bernhard Schoelkopf and Alexander J. Smola

topics.name: Gaussian Processes and Bayesian Nonparametrics
topics.definition: A Gaussian process puts a distribution over functions specified by a mean and a covariance kernel, giving closed-form Bayesian predictions; Bayesian nonparametrics, such as Dirichlet process mixtures, let model capacity grow with the data rather than fixing the number of components in advance.
topics.explanation: A GP marginalises to a multivariate Gaussian on any finite set of inputs, so exact regression has a predictive mean that interpolates the training data and a predictive variance that quantifies uncertainty; the entire modelling choice is the covariance function, whose form (linear, periodic, Matern, spectral mixture) encodes smoothness, stationarity and differentiability, and whose hyperparameters are learned by maximising the marginal likelihood (model evidence), an Occam-style criterion. Non-Gaussian likelihoods, notably classification, destroy analytic posterior inference and force approximations such as Laplace, expectation propagation or variational methods, and exact GPs cost O(n^3), driving sparse inducing-point approximations that connect to low-rank kernel methods. On the nonparametric side, a Dirichlet process is a prior over distributions whose concentration parameter controls diversity, exposed through the Blackwell-MacQueen urn, the Chinese restaurant process and stick-breaking, and a Dirichlet process mixture model infers an unknown, growing number of clusters, with the Pitman-Yor and Indian-buffet variants generalising to power-law and feature-models. The two halves share a theme: rather than choosing a point estimate from a fixed model class, one places a prior over richer function or distribution spaces and lets the data and the marginal likelihood select effective complexity.
learning_objectives: Derive the GP predictive posterior for regression from joint Gaussian conditioning.
Explain how kernel choice induces smoothness and stationarity priors.
Use the marginal likelihood for hyperparameter learning and relate it to model comparison.
Name the main GP inference approximations and the scalability problem.
Describe the Dirichlet process via the Chinese restaurant and stick-breaking constructions.
Write a truncated DP mixture and its Gibbs sampler.
math_foundations: Exchangeability and de Finetti measure for DP priors
common_misconceptions: GP inference is always exact (non-Gaussian likelihoods require approximations).
A Dirichlet process lets you sample infinitely many parameters directly (computationally one must truncate or use urn samplers).
A GP is just another kernel predictor (it returns a full posterior over functions with calibrated uncertainty).

further_reading.authors: Carl Edward Rasmussen and Christopher K. I. Williams

subdomains.name: Trees, Ensembles and Instance-Based Methods
subdomains.summary: Recursive partitioning and its ensembles, and the distance-driven neighbourhood, density and clustering methods that operate directly on examples.

topics.name: Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods
topics.definition: Decision trees recursively partition feature space to make locally constant predictions, while ensembles combine many learners, bagging to reduce variance and boosting to reduce bias, so random forests and gradient boosting have become the default strong learners for tabular data.
topics.explanation: A single classification or regression tree greedily selects axis-aligned splits that reduce impurity (Gini/entropy for labels, squared error for values) and is grown then pruned with cost-complexity regularisation; used alone it is low-bias but very high-variance because small data changes can restructure the whole tree. Bagging resamples the data and averages base learners to damp this variance, and random forests add random feature subsets at each split to decorrelate the trees, yielding out-of-bag generalisation estimates and (noisy) variable-importance measures. Boosting instead builds models sequentially, AdaBoost reweighting misclassified points and minimising an exponential-loss margin bound, while gradient boosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of a differentiable loss in function space, which recovers least-squares, logistic and quantile objectives from one template. Modern engines engineer this template for speed and regularisation: XGBoost adds a second-order approximation with explicit tree-complexity penalties and shrinkage, LightGBM grows leaves rather than levels with histogram-based splits and gradient/feature binning, and CatBoost uses ordered boosting to reduce prediction-shift bias and native categorical handling. The family is scale-invariant, handles missing values and non-linear interactions, extrapolates poorly and remains hard to beat on structured data.
learning_objectives: Compute impurity reduction and choose splits for a classification tree.
Explain how bagging reduces variance and how feature subsampling decorrelates trees.
Derive the AdaBoost weight update and interpret its margin view.
Frame gradient boosting as functional gradient descent and read off pseudo-residuals.
Identify the specific contributions of XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost.
Estimate generalisation with out-of-bag error.
math_foundations: Bootstrap sampling distribution and its averaging effect
Gradient in function space; negative gradient as pseudo-residual
common_misconceptions: Deep unpruned trees generalise (a lone tree overfits; pruning and ensembles are the fix).
Random-forest importance is an unbiased ranking (correlated features inflate it).
Boosting mainly reduces variance (it mainly reduces bias and can overfit with too many rounds).

topics.name: Clustering, Nearest-Neighbor, Density and Anomaly Methods
topics.definition: Instance-level structure is captured by partitioning points into groups (clustering), by predicting from nearby labelled points (nearest-neighbour), by estimating the input density (histograms, kernel density), and by flagging low-density or isolated points as anomalies.
topics.explanation: Centroid methods such as k-means, initialised by k-means++ and optimised by Lloyd iterations, minimise within-cluster variance and produce Voronoi cells but assume roughly spherical clusters and a known k, while k-medoids (PAM) use real exemplars and tolerate outliers. Hierarchical agglomerative clustering builds a dendrogram by merging under a linkage criterion (single, complete, average, Ward), letting one defer the choice of number of clusters; spectral clustering runs k-means in the coordinates of a graph Laplacian, capturing non-convex geometry, and DBSCAN/HDBSCAN group by density connectivity, discover arbitrarily shaped clusters and label noise. Mixture models with the expectation-maximisation algorithm give soft, likelihood-based clustering with principled model selection and monotone convergence to a local optimum. Nearest-neighbour prediction (Cover-Hart) is model-free and asymptotically bounded in error by the Bayes rate, but suffers the curse of dimensionality, driving exact indexes (kd/ball trees) and approximate search via locality-sensitive hashing. Kernel and histogram density estimation expose the bandwidth bias-variance tradeoff, and anomalies are detected by methods that score isolation or local density, from one-class SVM and local outlier factor to isolation forests. Validation relies on internal scores (silhouette, Davies-Bouldin) or, when available, external labels (adjusted Rand, mutual information).
learning_objectives: Run Lloyd's algorithm, state the k-means objective, and explain k-means++ seeding.
Compare linkage criteria and cut a dendrogram sensibly.
Explain DBSCAN's eps/minPts parameters and why it finds non-convex clusters.
Derive the EM updates for a Gaussian mixture and describe its convergence guarantee.
Analyze the kNN curse of dimensionality and the role of the distance metric.
Choose a bandwidth for kernel density estimation and detect anomalies.
math_foundations: Graph Laplacian eigenvectors for spectral embedding
Kernel bandwidth as a bias-variance knob
common_misconceptions: k-means recovers the true clusters (it assumes convex, equal-scale clusters and a preset k).
DBSCAN is parameter-free (eps and minPts dominate the result).
Euclidean distance in high dimensions is informative (concentration makes it nearly meaningless).
EM guarantees the global maximum (it converges only to a local one).

subdomains.name: Dimensionality Reduction and Manifold Learning
subdomains.summary: Projecting high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional space that preserves variance, neighbourhood structure, discriminative signal, or manifold geometry.

topics.name: Dimensionality Reduction and Manifold Learning
topics.definition: Dimensionality reduction maps high-dimensional data to a lower-dimensional space that preserves variance (linear), neighbourhood structure (graph/nonlinear) or discriminative information, and manifold learning models the data as lying on or near an intrinsically low-dimensional nonlinear surface.
topics.explanation: Principal component analysis finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; via the covariance eigen-decomposition it is exactly the optimal low-rank reconstruction guaranteed by Eckart-Young, so it is the linear workhorse for compression, denoising and visualisation, with kernel PCA, sparse PCA and probabilistic PCA extending it to nonlinear, selectable and likelihood-based settings. The supervised counterpart, linear discriminant analysis, instead maximises between-over-within scatter to build discriminative axes. Nonlinear spectral methods recover geometry from a neighbourhood graph: classical multidimensional scaling preserves pairwise distances, Isomap promotes geodesic graph distances to unwrap manifolds, and locally linear embedding stitches overlapping local affine charts. For visualization and structure t-SNE embeds conditional neighbour probabilities by minimising a Kullback-Leibler divergence (with perplexity as its effective neighbourhood size and Barnes-Hut scaling), while UMAP builds a fuzzy simplicial-set topological model and preserves more global structure. Autoencoders learn the same kind of nonlinear reduction with neural networks, and the whole area connects to the manifold hypothesis behind learned representations and to persistent homology for quantifying the topology one is trying to preserve. Crucially, a reduction is defined by what it claims to keep, so its axes and 2D plots must never be read as evidence of a structure the objective was not sensitive to.
learning_objectives: Derive PCA as variance maximisation and as the leading singular vectors of the centred data.
Relate PCA reconstruction error to the Eckart-Young theorem and the energy criterion for rank.
State the LDA between/within-scatter objective and how it differs from PCA.
Explain how MDS, Isomap and LLE recover manifold geometry from neighbourhoods.
Contrast t-SNE and UMAP and the meaning of perplexity and global structure.
Evaluate a reduction by preserved structure rather than by the plot's appearance.
math_foundations: Covariance eigen-decomposition / SVD of the centred matrix
Geodesic versus Euclidean distances on a neighbourhood graph
Intrinsic dimension and the manifold hypothesis
applications: Preprocessing for classical and deep learners
common_misconceptions: PCA finds the most discriminative directions (it maximises variance ignoring labels; LDA is supervised).
t-SNE cluster distances and sizes are quantitatively meaningful (it preserves mostly local structure).
Reducing dimensionality always improves downstream performance (it can destroy signal).

subdomains.name: Graphical Models and Bayesian Inference
subdomains.summary: Structured probabilistic models and the exact, approximate and Monte Carlo/variational inference used to reason and learn with them at the classical level.

topics.name: Probabilistic Graphical Models and Classical Bayesian Inference
topics.definition: Graphical models encode a joint distribution as a product of local factors guided by a graph's conditional independencies, and the same inference machinery, exact elimination, belief propagation, variational bounds and Monte Carlo, also powers classical Bayesian model learning and comparison.
topics.explanation: Directed Bayesian networks factor the joint along parent-child links while undirected Markov random fields and factor graphs express it through potential functions, and d-separation turns graph structure into a language of implied conditional independencies. Exact inference by variable elimination and by building a junction tree of cliques exploits factor sparsity but is governed by induced width, and MAP/counting inference in general graphs is #P-hard, so approximate inference is central: belief propagation is exact on trees and the popular loopy BP heuristic is otherwise, while variational inference reframes posterior approximation as minimising a KL divergence, equivalently maximising the evidence lower bound, via mean-field or coordinate-ascent updates that rest on convex duality. Monte Carlo estimation and Markov chain Monte Carlo (Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs) give unbiased samples when deterministic approximations are unreliable, and expectation-maximisation handles maximum-likelihood learning with latent variables by alternating a posterior E-step with a maximisation M-step, monotone in likelihood but only locally convergent. At the classical Bayesian level this unifies conjugate-posterior analysis, MAP with Laplace approximations, and posterior-predictive model comparison through the marginal likelihood, with information criteria connecting back to MDL. The shared skeleton, a graph, a factorised objective, and an optimisation-or-sampling scheme, is one of the most reusable templates in machine learning.
learning_objectives: Read implied independencies from a graph via d-separation.
Write the joint factorisation of a Bayesian network and of a Markov random field.
Run variable elimination and identify the induced-width cost.
Derive belief-propagation message updates and state the tree-exactness condition.
Formulate the ELBO and mean-field coordinate updates.
Write the EM algorithm and explain its monotone-likelihood, local-convergence behaviour.
Set up a Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs sampler and discuss convergence.
math_foundations: Detailed balance and ergodicity of MCMC
common_misconceptions: Loopy belief propagation is guaranteed to converge and be exact (it is exact only on trees).
A Bayesian network's edges assert causality (a factorisation is not causal; see causal-inference-foundations).
EM always reaches the global optimum (it converges to a stationary point).

subdomains.name: The Modelling Workflow: Features, Validation and Interpretation
subdomains.summary: The disciplined pipeline from raw inputs to a trusted, well-chosen, and explainable model.

topics.name: Feature Engineering, Selection and Preprocessing
topics.definition: Feature engineering transforms raw data into informative representations and selects the subset worth keeping, while preprocessing standardises, encodes and imputes so models receive a well-conditioned, leakage-free input.
topics.explanation: Representation is often more decisive than model choice: polynomial and interaction terms, binning, domain ratios, and learned embeddings reshape what a linear or tree learner can express. Scaling (standardisation, min-max) matters for gradient and distance methods but not for trees; categorical variables require encoding (one-hot, ordinal for true ordering, frequency or target encoding with care to avoid leakage), and text/image pipelines compress unstructured inputs to numeric features. Feature selection improves interpretability, latency and sometimes accuracy, and divides into filter methods scoring each feature with correlation, mutual information or ANOVA, wrapper methods (forward/backward selection, recursive feature elimination) evaluating subsets with a model, and embedded methods that select during fitting via L1 sparsity or tree importances, each trading statistical soundness against cost. Missingness must be classified by mechanism, MCAR/MAR/MNAR, because the safe treatment differs, from mean/median and nearest-neighbour or iterative MICE imputation to explicit missing-indicator features, and naive mean-filling can bias estimates. Through it all the governing discipline is to fit every transformation on the training split only and apply it to held-out data, preventing data leakage; ill-conditioning from poor scaling or near-duplicate features degrades optimisation and connects to the numerical-stability material of the mathematics domain.
learning_objectives: Construct informative features and choose a categorical encoding that avoids leakage.
Classify filter, wrapper and embedded selection and trade off their cost and soundness.
Distinguish MCAR, MAR and MNAR and select an appropriate imputation strategy.
Prevent data leakage by fitting preprocessing inside the cross-validation loop.
Explain how scaling affects distance/gradient methods and conditioning.
math_foundations: Condition number and the effect of scaling on optimisation
common_misconceptions: Fitting the scaler on the whole dataset before splitting is harmless (it leaks test information).
Imputation is always benign (MNAR imputation biases estimates).
More features are better (irrelevant and redundant features hurt variance and conditioning).

topics.name: Model Selection, Validation and Interpretation
topics.definition: Model selection picks a learner and its hyper-parameters to maximise expected test performance without overfitting the validation signal, and interpretation exposes which features actually drive a model's predictions.
topics.explanation: Estimating generalisation is the core problem: a single hold-out is high-variance, so k-fold, stratified, leave-one-out and repeated/grouped cross-validation are used, and when hyper-parameters are tuned the whole tuning procedure must sit inside the validation loop (nested cross-validation) or the reported score is optimistic leakage. Criteria translate fit into penalised complexity, AIC, BIC and deviance being sample versions of an information-theoretic/minimum-description-length tradeoff. Hyper-parameter search runs from grid and random to Bayesian optimisation over the configuration space, and honest practice recognises selection overfitting: choosing the best of many candidates inflates apparent performance, a multiple-comparisons problem that the inference-and-experimentation topic of the mathematics domain formalises. Interpretation then audits the chosen model: partial-dependence and accumulated-local-effect plots expose marginal and interaction structure, permutation importance measures global reliance, and LIME and SHAP give local, additive explanations, the latter grounded in Shapley values from cooperative game theory, which also guarantee uniqueness. These are model-agnostic trust and communication tools with a hard limit, association in the model is not causality, and they complement, not replace, careful validation.
learning_objectives: Compare k-fold, LOO and stratified/grouped CV by bias and variance of the estimate.
Explain why hyper-parameter tuning must be nested inside CV.
Compute AIC/BIC and connect them to MDL and KL-based model choice.
Run permutation importance and interpret a SHAP/additive explanation.
Identify selection overfitting and the multiple-comparisons risk in benchmarking.
Distinguish global from local interpretation and state the association-not-causation limit.
math_foundations: Bias-variance of the CV estimate and optimism
KL divergence as the basis of information criteria
Multiplicity corrections for selecting the best model
common_misconceptions: Tuning on the test set is acceptable (it is leakage that yields optimistic scores).
The best validation score is a fair estimate of test performance (selection overfitting inflates it).
A high feature importance proves that feature causes the outcome (importance is model-association, not causation).

notes_on_gaps: Count: 48 topics across three domains (mathematical-foundations 34, foundations-of-machine-learning 5, classical-machine-learning 9). The three-part scope assigned to this area enumerates a wider breadth than the nominal 25-45-topic band, so rather than stub or drop explicitly-demanded topics I kept each domain complete and made the two ML domains as compact as genuine substance allowed: each classical-ML topic deliberately aggregates a cluster of closely related methods the way ESL/PRML/PML organise chapters (for example linear+GLM+naive-Bayes, or trees+bagging+boosting), and paradigms such as multi-instance, curriculum, weakly-supervised and representation/metric learning are folded into their nearest topic rather than split into stubs. Federated and distributed learning is covered at the optimisation level by mathematical-foundations/distributed-and-federated-optimization and at the paradigm level by foundations-of-machine-learning/dataset-shift-noisy-labels-imbalance-and-federated-learning; a deep-learning-specific federated/privacy topic is left to the deep-learning area. To avoid slug collisions, generalization-theory, self-supervised-learning, variational-inference, markov-chain-monte-carlo, monte-carlo-methods, causal-inference-foundations, transformer/VAE/GAN/normalizing-flow/diffusion topics and all RL topics are treated as shared cross-area slugs and only referenced, never redefined; generalization-theory is substantively delivered here through mathematical-foundations/statistical-learning-theory and .../minimax-rates-no-free-lunch-and-pac-bayes. Deep learning itself (backpropagation, CNNs/RNNs, transformers, generative models, RL, sequence modelling, tokenization, GNNs) is intentionally out of this half. Algebraic geometry (shared algebraic-geometry-ml) and stochastic calculus (shared stochastic-calculus) are referenced elsewhere and not developed here. Citation honesty: standard textbooks and their years were relied on from established knowledge, while a minority of conference-paper entries carry only the title/authors and venue-year I am confident about with url set to null and an et al. for long author lists; lesson authors must confirm exact venues/DOIs/URLs before publishing. Open or speculative points flagged inside topics rather than asserted as settled include generalisation guarantees for continual/lifelong learning (catastrophic forgetting remains unsolved), the practical usability of untruncated Bayesian nonparametrics, and whether internal clustering-validity indices certify meaningful partitions.
